summary: Full Steam Ahead: much more Steam (versions, DLC, achievements, friends, the Workshop), Amazon Games, Restart game, and fixes for American Truck Simulator, Megabonk and Counter-Strike 2.
added: Amazon Games in the Stores tab: sign in on Amazon's own page and install the games you bought or claimed with Prime Gaming. Files come straight from Amazon's servers and are checked against Amazon's signed file list.

Steam: a Version and DLC row on a game's page. Pick another version Steam offers (a beta or the previous version), type a beta password for a private beta, and turn DLC you own on or off. Only the parts that differ are downloaded.

Steam: achievements with pictures, descriptions, unlock dates and how many players have them, a progress line ("12 of 50 unlocked") on the game's page, pop-ups when you unlock one in a game, and the full list in the in-game menu (Steam > Achievements).

Steam: your friends (read only): who is playing what, who is online, and who was last seen when, on a Friends button at the top right of the Home screen, in the Steam list and in the in-game menu, plus a Friends playing row on a game's page. Nothing is sent to Porthole's servers.
Steam: news and patch notes for a game, and Steam's review score and Steam Deck rating on its page (public Steam pages, no sign-in).

Steam Workshop (beta): browse, search, subscribe to and download a game's items in the app and inside the running game (in-game menu > Steam). Items are checked for updates when a game's page opens (switch it off with Update mods automatically). Depot items such as American Truck Simulator mods can be subscribed to while a game runs and download when it closes. Tested with Portal 2 and American Truck Simulator.

Restart game, in the in-game menu and on the Workshop page: closes the game and Porthole, then starts the same game again when you open Porthole (iOS needs one tap on a notification). If a game ignores the close request, Porthole asks whether to stop it.
A Steam menu in the running game opens when a game asks for Steam's overlay (its own Workshop or Store button), instead of leaving the game stuck until you press Escape.
Your own VPN can come back as soon as JIT is on (Settings > JIT and tunnel), for networks that block Steam.
The launch screen says why Steam will not start a game (needs an update, or files marked damaged) and what to do, and says when Steam has not signed in.
Add a game > Import a game folder says how to choose the folder, and writes what happens to the log.
changed: Signing in to Steam starts with the QR code (approved in the Steam mobile app, so Porthole never handles your password). The sign-in screen says Porthole is unofficial and not affiliated with Valve.

Verify and update files on a Steam game's page really checks every file against Steam now and downloads only what is missing or damaged. Updating a game also keeps the parts of files already on the device that have not changed.
Megabonk starts without a hand-typed engine line and its controller works in Automatic. Sorting the all-games page by recently played now includes GOG and itch.io games.
Engine r17 (it was r13 in 1.0.1). Compatibility badges start empty for it.
fixed: American Truck Simulator (and other games that create a tiny placeholder window and rely on DirectX to size it) showed as a postage stamp. The window is now resized or made to cover the screen.
Megabonk, and any Unity game that uses Rewired's Windows.Gaming.Input plugin, saw no controller. The controller is now also offered as a Windows.Gaming.Input gamepad for these games.
Counter-Strike 2's first-person look stopped at a fixed angle. The game's mouse-input thread needs a system window class that was missing for the game, so it never got raw mouse movement.

Portal 2 and other single-file Workshop items are recorded the way Steam records them and put where Steam keeps finished downloads, so the game opens maps the app downloaded even where Steam's own download times out.

A Steam game is no longer started with too little memory room: on a bad start of the app the room for the game's translated code can shrink and the game runs out of memory a minute in. Porthole now stops, says so and offers Close Porthole.
Workshop single-file items downloaded from a web address (Portal 2 maps) no longer fail with "Steam did not accept the sign-in token".

summary: Counter-Strike 2 look: the missing Message window class (engine r17).
changed: Engine r17 (badges start empty for it).
fixed: Counter-Strike 2's first-person look stopped at a fixed angle in every control layout. The game's mouse-input thread needs a small hidden window of the system class "Message", and that class was only registered for the first program Porthole ran, not for the game started by Steam's client, so the window could not be created and the game never received raw mouse movement (it fell back to the pointer position, which stops at the screen edge). The Message class is now registered for every program. Needs a test on a device.

summary: A Steam game is not started with too little memory room.
fixed: Counter-Strike 2 and other Steam games failed a minute after starting with "the system ran out of memory" on some starts of the app. iOS places memory differently on every start of Porthole, and on a bad one it had put something where Porthole keeps the room for the game's translated code, so that room shrank (544 MB instead of about 900 MB) and ran out as the game loaded. Porthole now sees the small room before the game starts, stops, says so, and offers Close Porthole: open it again and start the game (it is different every time).

summary: Verify and update files only downloads what is missing or changed.
changed: "Verify and update files" on a Steam game's page now really checks every file against Steam (a few minutes for a big game) and downloads only the parts that are missing or damaged. Before, it never looked at the files: for a game that was up to date it did nothing, and for a game with a newer build it downloaded every file of the changed depot again.
fixed: Updating a Steam game (a newer build, a beta, DLC) no longer downloads files that are already on the device and unchanged: the parts of each file already on the disk are compared with Steam's list and kept.

summary: Launch screen says why Steam will not start a game.
fixed: When Valve's Steam client refuses to start a game because its files are out of date or marked damaged (it cannot download in the game), the launch screen stayed on "Signing in to Steam". It now says "Steam won't start the game yet" and what to do: update the game under Stores > Steam (when a newer build is on Steam), or use Verify files under Details and files.

summary: Counter-Strike 2 look: more diagnostics.
added: A log line that names the window class a thread could not create (for Counter-Strike 2's mouse-input thread). Nothing else changes.

summary: Counter-Strike 2 look: fix attempt (engine r16).
changed: Engine r16 (badges start empty for it).
fixed: Counter-Strike 2's first-person look stopped at a fixed angle, in every control layout. The game's mouse-input thread is started late and could not create the small hidden window it needs (no usable desktop), so the game never received raw mouse movement and fell back to the pointer position, which stops at the screen edge. A thread with no usable desktop now gets the process's desktop, so the window is created and raw mouse input is registered. The steps are written to the log as [desktop-diag]. Needs a test on a device.

summary: Workshop maps recorded the way Steam records them; window-creation diagnostics.
added: Log lines ([createwin] 0159) that show why a window cannot be created, to find why Counter-Strike 2's look stops at a fixed angle (its raw-input window is created and the thread ends at once). Nothing else about windows changes.
fixed: Single-file Workshop items (Portal 2 and Counter-Strike maps) are now recorded the way Steam's client records them (manifest -1 and the item's UGC handle). Before, Steam's client saw them as changed, marked the game "needs update", tried to download them itself and cleaned away the copy the app had put in its finished-download cache, so the game said the map was not downloaded. Items downloaded earlier are corrected when the app opens and when a game's page opens.

summary: Counter-Strike 2 look: diagnostics.
added: Log lines (look-diag) that show what a game registers for mouse input and how the first-person look reaches it, to find why Counter-Strike 2's look stops at a fixed angle. Nothing else changes.

summary: Portal 2 Workshop maps open when Steam's client can't download them itself.
fixed: Workshop maps that are a single file (Portal 2) did not open on a connection where Steam's client inside the game times out reaching the content server, even though the app had downloaded them. The app now also puts each map where Steam's client keeps a finished download (userdata/<account>/ugc/referenced/<id>/, with the data.vdf file Steam writes), so the game finds it. Maps already downloaded are filled in when the app opens and when a game's page opens. Needs Steam to be signed in; nothing is sent anywhere new.

summary: Restart game when a game ignores the close request.
fixed: Restart game did nothing with a game that ignores the close request (Alt+F4), such as Portal 2: the game kept running and Porthole waited for it. It now sends the request twice, and if the game has not closed after 8 seconds asks whether to stop it and restart (Keep playing / Stop and restart). The steps are written to the log as [restart].

summary: Importing a game folder is explained and logged.
added: The steps of importing a game folder (the picker opened or closed, the folder chosen, how many files, errors) are now written to the log, so a report about a folder that "won't select" shows what happened.
changed: Add a game > Import a game folder now says how to choose the folder: in Files, open the game's folder, then tap Open at the top right. Tapping a folder only goes into it; Open chooses the folder you are in.

summary: Achievement progress on the game pages.
added: The Achievements row on a Steam game's page (in the Stores tab and in the library) now says how many you have, for example "12 of 50 unlocked" or "All 50 unlocked", without opening the list. It is read when the page opens (at most once an hour per game) and kept on the device only; signing out forgets it.

summary: News and Deck rating on Steam store pages.
added: The News and patch notes row and the Steam Deck rating chip are now also on a game's page in the Stores tab (the page you see before installing), not only on installed games' pages in the library.

summary: Steam news, review score and Deck rating.
added: A News and patch notes row on a Steam game's page: the game's official announcements and patch notes from Steam, newest first, with a link to read each on Steam. The same list is in the in-game menu (Steam > News), where it only reads.

Two chips on a Steam game's page: Steam's review summary (for example Overwhelmingly Positive, 99%) and its Steam Deck rating (Verified, Playable or Unsupported). The Deck rating is Valve's test on a Steam Deck, not a promise about how the game runs in Porthole.
These come from Steam's public pages. No sign-in is used and only the game's number is sent.

summary: Restart game.
added: Restart game, in the in-game menu (Session) and on the Workshop page when a mod has just arrived or is waiting for the game to close. It closes the game the usual way (so it can save), closes Porthole, and sends a notification: tap it, or open Porthole yourself within 30 minutes, and the same game starts again after the Workshop downloads that were waiting have finished (up to two minutes). A notice on the Home screen shows it and has a Cancel button. iOS does not let an app reopen itself, which is why the notification is needed.

summary: Workshop updates are found and downloaded by themselves.
added: When you open a Steam game's page, Porthole checks whether any Workshop item you are subscribed to is missing or has a newer version on Steam, and downloads it (at most every 5 minutes per game, and not while a game is running). The Workshop row on the game page says "N updates available" when it is only counting. A new switch on the Workshop page, Update mods automatically, turns the automatic download off; the button below it still updates on demand.
changed: Opening a game's Workshop page only downloads missing and updated items by itself when Update mods automatically is on.

summary: Friends playing this game.
added: On a Steam game's page, a Friends playing row shows which of your Steam friends are in that game right now (for example "2 playing now"), and opens the list of who they are. Read only, from the friends list the app already loads.

summary: Friends button on the Home Screen.
added: A Friends button at the top right of the Home Screen, always visible there (and only there, not on a game's page). It opens your Steam friends list and shows how many are online once the list has loaded. If you are not signed in to Steam it offers to open Steam to sign in.

summary: Steam friends list (test build).
added: Your Steam friends, read only: who is playing what, who is online, and (folded away) who is offline, with their picture and how long ago they were last seen. It is on the Steam game list (the Friends button next to Sort) and in the in-game menu (Steam > Friends). It refreshes every 45 seconds while it is open. Names, pictures and status come from Steam with the sign-in the app already has; nothing is sent to Porthole's servers and the list is kept in memory only. Ignored, blocked and pending people are not shown.
changed: The friends probe from the last two test builds is gone.

summary: Friends list probe, second try (log lines only, test build).
changed: Test build: the friends probe now reads the ids the way Steam writes them. Log lines only.

summary: Friends list probe (log lines only, test build).
changed: Test build for the friends list. Twenty seconds after the app opens (when you are signed in to Steam) it asks Steam three ways for your friends' names and online state and writes only counts and field names to the log. Nothing is shown in the app and no friend's name or id is logged.

summary: Wording of the Steam-not-reachable message (test build).
changed: The launch screen's message when Steam has not signed in now just asks you to check your internet connection.

summary: The launch screen says when Steam cannot be reached (test build).
added: When a Steam game's launch is stuck because Steam has not signed in (usually a network that blocks Steam), the launch screen now says so after a short wait (about 12 seconds when Porthole's own connection to Steam also failed, otherwise about 40) and suggests your VPN, cellular data or another Wi-Fi. Before, it just kept saying it was waiting. The wait is also written to the log.

summary: Workshop downloads survive closing the app (test build).
fixed: Workshop items that were waiting or downloading when the app closed (the app closes itself after a game, and you may force-quit it) are remembered and start again the next time the app opens. In build 1.1.26 the waiting list was only picked up once a Workshop screen was opened.

summary: Workshop items wait for the game to close and then download (test build).
added: A Workshop item that is kept in the game's Workshop depot (such as an American Truck Simulator mod) can be subscribed to while a game is running: it shows 'Subscribed, downloads when the game closes' and starts by itself when the game ends. The waiting list is kept if the app is closed, and an item Steam's own client already fetched at the same version is not downloaded again.
fixed: A Workshop download that was running when a game started no longer ends as an error; it waits for the game to close and continues.

summary: Steam: QR sign-in first, and Porthole no longer writes into Steam's download cache (test build).
changed: Signing in to Steam now starts with the QR code, which you approve in the Steam mobile app, so the app never handles your password; the account-name-and-password form is one tap away. The sign-in screen says that Porthole is unofficial and not affiliated with Valve.

Porthole no longer puts a copy of a downloaded single-file Workshop item (such as a Portal 2 map) into Steam's own download cache. Steam's client downloads the item itself, and the app's own copy in the Workshop folder stays.

summary: Workshop notice updated (test build).
changed: The Workshop beta notice now says which games are known to work (Portal 2 maps, American Truck Simulator mods) instead of saying older games have not worked.

summary: A game's Steam overlay request opens the Steam menu (test build).
added: When a Steam game asks for Steam's overlay (its Workshop or Store button, or Shift+Tab), the in-game Steam menu opens at the Workshop instead, and an Escape press is sent to close the overlay's empty screen. Before, the overlay could not draw and the game stopped answering until you pressed Escape. There is a switch for it in the Steam tab (Open this menu instead).

summary: Your VPN comes back as soon as JIT is on (test build).
added: Settings > JIT and tunnel > Your own VPN: 'Turn it back on as soon as JIT is on' (on by default, needs the shortcut that turns your VPN back on). The VPN Porthole pauses for its tunnel now comes back right after JIT is switched on, before the game starts, instead of when the game closes. This is for networks that block Steam: the game's Steam sign-in now goes through your VPN. Porthole leaves the app for a moment to run the shortcut, as it does for cellular data, and waits for the VPN to be up.

summary: All achievements in the in-game menu (test build).
added: The in-game menu's Steam tab has an Achievements part: every achievement of the game you are playing with its picture, description, when you unlocked it and how common it is, with the unlocked ones first. It is read from the files Steam's client keeps on the device, so it works in the game and updates while the menu is open. The pop-up switch and test button moved there.

summary: Pop-ups for unlocked Steam achievements (test build).
added: While a Steam game runs, an achievement that Steam records for it shows as a pop-up at the top of the screen with its picture, name and description. The app reads the stats file Steam's client keeps on the device, so it needs no connection, and it ignores history Steam syncs at the start of a game. In the in-game menu's Steam tab there is a switch for the pop-ups and a button that shows a test pop-up.
changed: The test probes of the Steam work (Web API reads and file watching at game start) are gone.

summary: Windows that rely on DirectX to size them (American Truck Simulator) - test build, new engine.
changed: Test build with a new engine (r15). When a game asks DirectX to resize its window or to go full screen, the window is now resized or covers the screen as it would on Windows, if it does not already. American Truck Simulator creates a tiny placeholder window and relied on this, so it showed as a postage stamp. Games whose window already has the right size are left as they were. Compatibility badges start fresh for the new engine.

summary: Window requests in the log (test build).
changed: Test build: the first 150 position, size, show and style requests a program makes for its top-level windows are written to the log as [winreq] 0156, to find out why American Truck Simulator's window stays tiny. Nothing else changes.

summary: Windows that start tiny (American Truck Simulator) - test build, new engine.
changed: Test build with a new engine (r14). A program that asks for a default-size window can no longer end up with a 132x38 one: the size now comes from the start-up size when it is usable, else 3/4 of the work area, else 3/4 of the screen. Every window request is written to the log as [createwin] 0156 so the cause of American Truck Simulator's tiny window can be read from it. Compatibility badges start fresh for the new engine.

summary: Workshop marked as beta (test build).
added: The Workshop rows (on a Steam game's page and its library page) and the Workshop part of the in-game Steam tab now carry a Beta badge. The first time you open the Workshop in the app or in a game, a notice says it is mostly untested, that only a few games have been tried and that older games have not worked so far.

summary: Steam tab in the in-game menu; older Workshop items download while a game runs (test build).
changed: The in-game menu's Workshop tab is now called Steam, and holds the Workshop; friends and chat will join it there.
fixed: Workshop items that are a file at a web address (such as Portal 2 maps) no longer fail in the game with 'This item downloads when the game is closed'; only items kept in the game's Workshop depot wait for the game to close.

summary: Steam Workshop inside the game (test build).
added: The in-game menu has a Workshop tab for Steam games (when you are signed in to Steam): see the Workshop items on the device, browse and search the game's items, subscribe and download, tap an installed item twice to remove it. While a game runs it uses only Steam's web calls and plain file downloads; items kept in the game's Workshop depot download after the game is closed.
changed: Downloads of older Workshop items try up to eight times (alternating between Steam's two names for the server) before giving up.

summary: Steam Workshop: network details in the log (test build).
changed: Test build: each download of an older Workshop item writes one line to the log saying which server address it reached, over IPv4 or IPv6, with which protocol and how long each step took, to find out why Steam's user-content server drops connections on some networks.

summary: Steam Workshop: downloads of older items retry on the other Steam address (test build).
fixed: Workshop items that are a file at a web address failed with 'No internet connection' when the connection to Steam's user-content server was dropped. The download now retries, alternating between Steam's two names for that server, before giving up.

summary: Steam Workshop: older items are also put where Steam's client looks (test build).
changed: Workshop items that are a single file at a web address (such as Portal 2 maps) are now also copied into Steam's own download cache for your account, with the details file Steam keeps, because the game asks Steam's client for them and the client could not download them itself. Removing the item removes that copy. Items already downloaded are fetched again the next time you open that game's Workshop list.

summary: Steam Workshop: older items (such as Portal 2 maps) download (test build).
fixed: Workshop: items that are a file at a web address, like most Portal 2 maps, are now downloaded from that address; before, the app tried the game's depot and failed. Looking an item up no longer fails with 'Steam did not accept the sign-in token', and trying again after a failure reuses what the app already knows about the item.

summary: Steam: Workshop in the app (test build).
added: A Workshop row on a Steam game's page and on its page in the library (when you are signed in to Steam): see the items you are subscribed to, browse a game's Workshop by trending, newest, most subscribed or top rated, search it, and subscribe or unsubscribe. Subscribing happens on your Steam account and the item's files are downloaded into the game's Steam folder (steamapps/workshop) with the record Steam's own client keeps. Opening the list downloads subscribed items that are missing or out of date.

summary: Steam: achievement pictures (test build).
fixed: Steam achievement pictures: the picture address no longer gets a second .jpg, and it now uses Steam's current picture server. A picture that still cannot load shows a trophy instead of an empty square.

summary: Steam: Achievements row also on a game's own page in the library (test build).
added: The Achievements row is now also on a Steam game's page in your library, not only on its Steam page.

summary: Steam: see your achievements for a game (test build).
added: On a Steam game's page, an Achievements row (when you are signed in to Steam) lists the game's achievements with their pictures, when you unlocked each one and how many players have it. Hidden achievements stay hidden until you unlock them. It only reads what Steam has recorded for your account; nothing is changed.

summary: Steam: choose a version (beta) of a game and its DLC (test build).
added: On a Steam game's page, a Version and DLC row (when you are signed in to Steam): pick another version of the game that Steam offers, such as a beta or the previous version, or type a beta password to open a private one; turn DLC you own on or off. Download changes fetches only what differs, so adding DLC does not download the game again.
changed: DLC you own is now installed with a Steam game, as Steam does, unless you turn it off on the game's page. Games already installed get it the next time you update them.
A Steam game's files record (appmanifest) now lists DLC depots with their DLC app, and a beta version carries a BetaKey, so Valve's client treats the files as that version.

summary: Steam branch: the test probes also list which of your games have Workshop items (log lines only).
changed: Test build for the Steam feature work. The probes from 1.1.3 now also check each game you own, a few per second, for Workshop items and write one line to the log listing the games that have any. Nothing is shown in the app and nothing on your account is changed.

summary: Steam branch: test probes for friends, achievements and Workshop (log lines only).
changed: Test build for the Steam feature work. When a Steam game starts, Porthole reads (never changes) a few things from Steam's web service with the sign-in it already holds and writes only counts and public item names to the log: friends, achievements and Workshop items. While the game runs it also logs which of Steam's own files change. Nothing is shown in the app.

summary: Amazon Games joins the stores, and Megabonk starts and sees the controller by itself.
added: Amazon Games in the Stores tab: sign in on Amazon's own page and install the games you bought on Amazon or claimed with Prime Gaming. Files come straight from Amazon's servers and are checked against Amazon's signed file list. Some Prime games need Amazon's online services and may not start.
changed: Megabonk now starts without a hand-typed engine line (real thread suspension is switched on for it), and its controller works in Automatic.
Sorting the all-games page by recently played now includes GOG and itch.io games.
fixed: Unity games that use Rewired's Windows.Gaming.Input plugin (Megabonk) saw no controller in any mode but keyboard and mouse: the plugin only asks for gamepads, and the pad was not one. The controller is now also offered as a Windows.Gaming.Input gamepad for these games, and Automatic keeps the Xbox pad for them instead of showing a PlayStation controller as a DualSense. A line of your own (env.MADEIRA_WGI_HOST_PADS) still wins.

summary: Megabonk starts and sees the controller by itself, and so does any game that reads its pad through Rewired (private test build).
changed: Megabonk now starts without a hand-typed engine line (real thread suspension is switched on for it), and its controller works in Automatic.
fixed: Unity games that use Rewired's Windows.Gaming.Input plugin (Megabonk) saw no controller in any mode but keyboard and mouse: the plugin only asks for gamepads, and the pad was not one. The controller is now also offered as a Windows.Gaming.Input gamepad for these games, and Automatic keeps the Xbox pad for them instead of showing a PlayStation controller as a DualSense. A line of your own (env.MADEIRA_WGI_HOST_PADS) still wins.

summary: BeamNG.drive starts and can be played (early support).
added: BeamNG.drive (Steam, version 0.39.4.0) starts, shows its menus, loads maps and drives. It needs one extra file that Porthole cannot supply: Ultralight's ICU data, icudt67l.dat, copied into the game's ultralight folder. docs/GAME_FIXES.md says where to get it and where it goes.

A BeamNG.drive game fix, applied automatically: the game is started with its own switch for the menu engine that does not use Chromium (-forceUltralight), and the memory layout, no-copy image loading and lock settings it needs are set for that launch only.
changed: New game engine version (279fd0f-r13): compatibility badges start fresh for it, and older reports stay visible as earlier ones. Most of the engine changes are switched on only for BeamNG.drive's launch; the monitor fix below applies to every game.
Game fixes that set a file aside now also apply to games started through Steam, and match the file name whatever its capitals; the log says where a fix looked when it found nothing.
fixed: Borderless and fullscreen windows: a game that asks Windows for its monitor with a handle the engine does not know now gets the screen's size instead of an error. BeamNG.drive set its window to 0 by 0 in Borderless and showed an empty desktop with sound.

summary: Porthole 1.0.0: the first public release.
added: Windows PC games on iPhone and iPad, using the Madeira runtime (Wine, FEX and DXMT): a game library with art, play time, per-game settings and on-screen or controller controls.
Four stores in one Stores tab: sign in to Steam, Epic Games, GOG or itch.io and download the games you own, with one Downloads page, pause and resume, and a lock-screen download card.
A community compatibility list: badges from reports by other people, counted per device model and engine version, and a short report of your own in under a minute.
An in-game side-panel menu with power modes, frame generation, controller choice and an optional performance overlay, plus short guides and a first-game tour.
Updates from inside the app with your own certificate, checked against the maintainer's release signature, with every earlier version available to go back to.
JIT switched on from inside the app (on iOS 27 or later the pairing file is made on the device), and an optional private link so it needs no computer.

summary: Steam games whose launch number Valve's client does not know (PEAK) start again.
fixed: A Steam game could fail to start with Steam's "entry for launch option 0 not found" because Valve's client looks the launch number up in its own older copy of the game's information. Porthole now reads that copy (appcache/appinfo.vdf) and, when it does not have our number, asks for one it has. The log shows both lists ([dock] Valve's cached launch entries …).

summary: GOG and itch.io downloads fetch ahead with many requests at once.
changed: GOG's own-depot downloads keep a look-ahead window of chunks in flight (12 to start, up to 48 as the connection allows) and decode them in parallel, instead of four at a time with a wait for the slowest, and the small files of a container are fetched ahead too instead of one chunk after the other. Files are no longer synced to disk one by one (each is checked against GOG's checksum first).

itch.io uploads (and the installer files of older GOG games) are fetched as many byte-range requests at once when the server allows it, written in order, so an interrupted download still resumes where it stopped. A server without range support gets the single stream as before.
Unpacking for GOG and itch.io runs at normal priority, like Steam and Epic.

summary: Steam and Epic downloads unpack at normal priority again.
changed: Since 0.50.249 the unpacking, hash checking and writing of downloaded chunks ran at the lowest background priority, which on a fast connection made the phone's slower cores the limit (Steam went from 50-80 MB/s to 30-45). They run at user-initiated priority again; the throttled progress redraws stay.

summary: Epic Games downloads fetch ahead and run many chunks at once, like the Steam downloader.
changed: Epic downloads were 2-3 times slower than Steam's: they fetched four chunks, waited for the slowest, then the next four, and read each one back from a temporary file. They now keep a sliding window of chunks in flight (12 to start, up to 48 as the connection allows, 96 MB of look-ahead), decompress them in parallel, hold the data in memory and no longer sync every file to disk (a resumed install still checks every file's SHA-1).

summary: The new call/return shortcut is off by default again.
changed: Upstream's call/return stack removal (faster in The Forest) is off unless a game turns it on with env.MADEIRA_FEX_CALLRET_ELIDE = 1: Subnautica fails early with it.

summary: Fixes games that fail to start through Steam with "no package core" (Factorio) and other wrong directory listings.
fixed: A game started by Steam could be given another program's folder listing (Factorio's data folder came back as Steam's cloud-sync listing of its saves folder, so it found no game files). Each Wine process now has its own listing cache.

summary: The directory-listing trace leaves out Steam's own cache folders and keeps 3000 lines.
changed: env.MADEIRA_FILE_TRACE = 1: [dir-trace] no longer fills up with Steam's httpcache folders, and keeps up to 3000 lines (MADEIRA_FILE_TRACE_LIMIT).

summary: A directory-listing trace for engine lines (env.MADEIRA_FILE_TRACE = 1).
added: With env.MADEIRA_FILE_TRACE = 1 the log also lists every directory listing a game asks for ([dir-trace]: folder, what came back, the first names). For finding why a game does not see files that are there.

summary: Game details can change which program a game starts.
added: Game details > About > Program now has a Change button: pick another program from the game's folder (or type a path) without removing the game and adding it again. The game keeps its Steam link, compatibility record, settings, controls and play time.

summary: Fixes my merge in 0.50.373, which lost two engine defaults.
fixed: Fast synchronization's semaphore cells, interruptible waits and 20 ms park are on by default again (0.50.373 started games without them, which costs Unity games frames).
Two engine lines typed on one line (env.A = 0 env.B = 0) are read as two lines again.

summary: Engine update: 212 upstream Madeira commits merged (Madeira-merge branch, not yet tried on a device).
added: Upstream fixes now in the engine: misaligned atomics and unaligned ordered accesses, C++ throw repair, self-suspend waits, the wineserver doorbell, thread QoS kept, avail-phys, WGI host pads, cheaper dxmt render passes, and a call/return stack that costs nothing and takes 8 MiB less per thread.
changed: Where upstream had its own fix for something we fixed ourselves (alias pushes, JIT pool free list, x18 patcher, dxmt state swap, d2d1 DC read-back) upstream's version is used.

summary: Steam's PlayStation controller switch is turned on (with Steam's controller support downloaded), and the log shows Steam's controller switches.
added: Before a Steam game starts the log lists the SteamController_* switches in Steam's config files. With Steam's controller support downloaded and a PlayStation controller in use, Porthole sets SteamController_PS4Support = 1 in Steam's config.vdf so Steam's controller layer opens the pad instead of only probing it. env.PORTHOLE_STEAM_PS = 0 leaves the file alone.

summary: With Steam's controller support downloaded, a PlayStation controller is shown to Steam as a DualSense so Steam Input can find it.
changed: Once the Steam page's 'Steam controller support' is downloaded, a PlayStation controller connected as a Steam game starts is shown to the game and to Steam as a DualSense (with the Xbox pad kept). Steam's controller layer now starts (the 64-bit SDL3.dll loads) and looks for HID gamepads; before, Porthole hid the DualSense from Steam launches.

summary: A Steam controller download for games that read their controller through Steam, and Source games no longer start as keyboard and mouse.
added: Steam page > Steam controller support (Download): fetches the one 64-bit library Steam's own controller layer (Steam Input) was missing, about 1.3 MB from Valve's server, checked against its fingerprint first. Steam failed to load its SDL3.dll in every run, so games that take their pad from Steam Input (Portal, Portal 2) got no controller in any mode. Remove puts the original file back.
changed: Half-Life 2, Portal, Portal 2 and Left 4 Dead are back on Automatic: they no longer start with the controller as keyboard and mouse.

summary: Looking around with the controller's stick no longer spins the camera in games started through Steam, and Source-engine games start as keyboard and mouse.
changed: Half-Life 2 and its episodes, Portal, Portal 2 and Left 4 Dead 1 and 2 start with the controller as keyboard and mouse (the D-pad and sticks did nothing as an Xbox pad or a DirectInput joystick). If one of them reads the Xbox pad, Automatic switches it back. The automatic DirectInput joystick of 0.50.367 is gone; the game's Controller choice can still turn it on.
fixed: In games started through Steam, the stick that moves the mouse sent an absolute pointer even when the game had hidden the cursor for mouse look and put it back in the middle of the screen every frame, so the view spun at full speed. While the game hides its cursor the stick now sends relative movement.

summary: The 'Xbox and DirectInput joystick' choice no longer switches the DualSense off a second after the game starts.
fixed: With the game's Controller choice on 'Xbox and DirectInput joystick' and a HID controller type set app-wide, the first live controller update (about a second into the game) turned the DualSense off and left only the Xbox pad. That choice now leaves the DualSense as the session started it.

summary: Portal, Portal 2 and the other Source-engine games now find the controller through DirectInput.
changed: Half-Life 2 (and its episodes and Lost Coast), Portal, Portal 2 and Left 4 Dead 1 and 2 look for their controller through DirectInput, where the Xbox pad did not exist, so they never saw one. The pad is now also offered to them as a DirectInput joystick by itself (a game's own Controller choice still wins), and the log traces what the game asks DirectInput for.

summary: Games started through Steam keep the Xbox pad, so Steam Input cannot take a PlayStation controller away from them.
changed: A PlayStation controller is no longer shown to the game as a DualSense when the game starts through the Steam client (Steam Input takes a HID gamepad for itself and leaves the game without one). Those games get the Xbox pad as before. A game's own Controller choice still wins, and env.PORTHOLE_PAD_IDENTITY = steam turns the DualSense back on for Steam launches.

summary: Pick the controller the game sees from the in-game menu, and change it while you play.
added: In-game menu > Controls > Controller: Automatic, Xbox controller, DualSense and Xbox, or Keyboard and mouse. The choice applies at once, is remembered for the game, and shows which controller is connected. The DualSense is available when a PlayStation controller was connected as the game started; otherwise the choice is saved for the next start and the menu says so.

summary: Porthole now knows which controller you hold: the guides name its buttons, and a PlayStation pad shows up as a DualSense in the game.
added: The bottom guide, the section tabs' LB / RB marks, the in-game menu hint and the button lists name the buttons as printed on the connected controller: a DualSense or DualShock 4 shows \u2715 \u25CB L1 R1 Options Create / Share, a Switch Pro pad its own letters, an Xbox pad A B LB RB Menu View. The guide also says which controller it found, and Settings > Controls shows it.

A PlayStation controller connected when a game starts is shown to the game as a DualSense (with the Xbox pad kept next to it), so the game can show PlayStation buttons. A game's own Controller choice wins; env.PORTHOLE_PAD_IDENTITY = 0 goes back to the Xbox pad only.

summary: The section tabs are changed with LB and RB or a tap only; the D-pad no longer goes up to them.
changed: The tab bar at the top of the app (and the tabs and close button of the in-game menu) are no longer D-pad targets: Up from the content does not land on them and Left / Right do not move along them. LB and RB switch the section, and a tap still works.

summary: While a game runs, the controller's Create / PS buttons no longer start a screenshot or a screen recording.
fixed: On a DualSense, holding Create (the button that opens Porthole's menu together with Options) started a screen recording, and any game that uses that button had the same trouble. While a game runs the app now asks iOS to leave the pad's Home, Options and Menu buttons alone, and gives them back when the game ends. The log says which were turned off.

summary: Remap a game's controller buttons, and the last system dialogs a controller could not reach are gone.
added: Game page > Engine > Controller > Remap buttons: choose which button the game sees for each button on your pad (swap A and B, a bumper on a trigger, a button off), with quick swaps. It applies while the pad is an Xbox or DualSense pad for the game.
Settings > Engine options > Controllers > Open the menu with the controller: Menu + View, both stick clicks, the PS / Xbox button, or off.
changed: The uninstall questions for GOG and itch.io games and the 'Cannot run that' message are now sheets the controller can answer (they were iOS dialogs).

summary: Open the in-game menu with the controller and use it with the D-pad.
added: Hold Menu + View (Options + Create on a DualSense) for half a second to open or close the in-game menu. While it is open the game sees a controller with nothing pressed; the D-pad moves, A presses, B or Menu closes, LB and RB change the tab, Left and Right change a slider.
A short note over the game, the first three times, says how to open the menu from the controller. env.PORTHOLE_PAD_MENU = l3r3, home or off changes the buttons.

summary: The log of a crashing game now includes the code that made the failing call and the memory its registers point at.
added: When a game's code faults, the log shows the bytes around the instruction that made the call and the memory the main registers point at (first two faults).

summary: A game's engine line can switch off the larger lookup cache of busy threads, to find out whether it is behind a crash.
added: Engine line env.MADEIRA_FEX_HOTL1 = 0 (the default is on): every thread keeps the smaller lookup cache of the translator.

summary: Two engine lines typed on one line are now two lines.
fixed: A game's engine lines such as 'env.A = 0 env.B = 0' on one line were read as one setting (A got the value '0 env.B = 0') and B never applied, with nothing in the log saying so. Each env. setting after other text on a line now starts its own line.

summary: A game that crashes on one of its worker threads now ends the session instead of leaving the last picture on screen.
fixed: When the program the app started died with a crash (for example an access violation on a worker thread), Wine's main thread kept waiting, so the session never ended and the screen stayed frozen on the last frame. The session now ends about 4 seconds after the crash is reported, and the log says 'the game stopped with error 0x...'.

summary: The log now carries what a Unity game writes to its own log while it runs.
added: While a game runs, Porthole copies new lines of its own log file (Player.log, output_log.txt) into the Porthole log as [game-log] lines, so a game that stops loading shows what it last said. env.PORTHOLE_GAME_LOG = 0 switches it off.

summary: A game's own engine line can now keep its large empty memory reservations out of the translator's address space.
added: Engine line env.MADEIRA_STEER_PA_FIRST = 1 (off by default): the big reserve-only memory blocks some games ask for go to the free address range instead of the one the translator needs for new threads. For games that freeze on their loading screen with 'the emulator address band is exhausted' in the log.

summary: Auto power mode reworked: it now runs at a locked 60 FPS until iOS slows the fast cores, then holds a steady 30 FPS for a while.
changed: Auto no longer drops into Battery saver (its Eco mode moved the game onto the slow cores and the frame rate fell to 12-22). It plays at a locked 60 FPS without the 120 Hz screen hold, switches to a steady 30 FPS for 60 seconds or more when iOS starts holding the fast cores back, then tries 60 again.
fixed: Auto could stay in its break for minutes because it waited for the heat pressure to reach nominal, which it rarely does during play.

summary: A new Auto power mode eases off by itself when iOS starts holding the phone's fast cores back.
added: Power mode Auto: plays as Balanced, and when iOS starts slowing the fast cores (or its heat pressure rises) it drops to Battery saver for 45 seconds or more, then comes back. Pick it in Settings, on a game's page or in the in-game menu.

summary: The Processor card in the in-game menu now shows how much processor energy the game has used.
added: The Processor card shows the processor energy the game has used since it started, and the log records it when the fast cores are first held back.

summary: The app now tells iOS it runs latency-critical foreground work, and the menu shows how much of the game runs on the fast cores.
added: The Processor card in the in-game menu shows how much of the game's work runs on the fast cores.
changed: While a game runs the app asks iOS to treat it as latency-critical, user-initiated work and gives the process the highest latency and throughput tiers (env.PORTHOLE_SCHED_HINTS = 0 turns this off).

summary: The app now declares itself a game so iOS can use Game Mode, and the log records why the processor may be slowed.
added: The app registers for iOS Game Mode (full-screen, highest priority for the game).
The log has a line every 15 seconds, and one when the clamp starts, with iOS's thermal pressure level, the battery's charge, temperature and current, and Low Power Mode.

summary: The in-game menu shows when iOS has slowed the phone's fast processor cores.
added: The in-game menu's Performance tab has a Processor card: green while the fast cores run free, red when iOS holds them at about 1.1 GHz, with how long and when it started. The log gets a line when the clamp starts and ends.

summary: The profile locates time in the translator's own code more precisely.
changed: Profile where the time goes now divides the time inside the engine's own libraries into finer pieces.

summary: The translator's lookup cache can grow larger for the busiest thread, so it misses far less.
changed: The translator's code lookup cache can now grow to four times its old size for a thread that keeps missing it (a thread's busiest part of the game's code), which saves CPU time and so heat and battery.

summary: The log now says what causes the translator's lookup-cache misses.
changed: The log's lookup-cache lines now also show whether misses come from conflicts and which addresses miss most.

summary: The render-pass timer in the profile now measures each pass correctly and estimates memory traffic.
changed: Profile where the time goes now measures how long each kind of render pass keeps the GPU busy, and estimates how much memory each one moves.

summary: The render-pass timer in the profile now starts on this GPU.
fixed: The GPU render-pass timing in Profile where the time goes asked for a timer buffer that was too large; it now fits.

summary: The profile also times every render pass on the GPU.
added: Profile where the time goes also logs how much GPU time each kind of render pass uses.

summary: The translator's shorter function-call code is now on by default.
changed: The x86 translator now uses shorter code for function calls and returns by default (less CPU for audio and call-heavy code, so less heat and battery use). Engine line env.MADEIRA_FEX_LEAN = 0 turns it off for a game.

summary: The log now says whether the translator's shorter call code is on.
changed: The log has a line at start-up that says whether the shorter function-call code of the translator is on.

summary: The x86 translator has a new, shorter way to do function calls and returns, off by default.
added: Engine line env.MADEIRA_FEX_LEAN = 1 makes the x86 translator emit shorter code for function calls and returns (off by default while it is tested).
changed: The translator is rebuilt from its source with a documented build.

summary: The profile also logs the translated code of the hottest places.
changed: Profile where the time goes also logs the translated code at the twelve hottest places, to see how instructions are translated.

summary: The profile also writes the machine code of the hottest functions to the log.
changed: Profile where the time goes also logs the instructions of the ten functions that use the most time, so they can be studied.

summary: A new engine setting, yield-mode, changes how games that wait by yielding the core behave; the profile separates yielding threads.
added: Engine line yield-mode = 1, 2 or 3 changes what the Windows yield call does (off by default).
changed: Profile where the time goes leaves threads that are only yielding out of its shares and tells how many there were.

summary: The profile shows who called each system wait, and which game function was running.
changed: Profile where the time goes lists the chain of callers for time spent in the system and the game function that was running at the time.

summary: A badge on the game screen shows while the profile runs and when its result is in the log.
added: While Profile where the time goes runs, a badge at the top of the game screen counts down, then says the result is being worked out, then that it is in the log.

summary: The profile no longer gets stuck while it works out the result.
fixed: Profile where the time goes could take minutes to produce its result; the search for unplaced code is now cached and limited to 8 seconds.

summary: The profile places far more of the time: code between linked blocks and the native code of Wine's own libraries.
changed: Profile where the time goes now also names where the time goes inside Wine's own libraries and finds the translated code that the first version could not place.

summary: The profile now names the game code that uses the time.
changed: Profile where the time goes now shows, for the busiest threads, which game modules and functions use the time and which code called them.

summary: Games that use many threads run faster: fast synchronisation now covers semaphores and interruptible waits by default.
changed: Fast synchronisation covers semaphores, interruptible single waits and waits of up to 20 ms by default. Games that used to hammer the engine's server with thread wake-ups put much less load on it (tested on one game: over twice the frame rate).

summary: An opt-in setting lets waits that can be interrupted use the fast synchronisation too.
added: Setting env.MADEIRA_FASTSYNC_ALERTABLE = 1 in a game's engine lines lets its interruptible waits use fast synchronisation (off by default).

summary: Fast synchronisation now really starts: the engine's server decided too early that it was off.
fixed: The fast synchronisation between a game's threads was never active on the server side, because the server decided before the setting was there; it now waits for the setting.

summary: A profile of where a game spends its time, from the in-game menu.
added: The in-game menu's Game tab has Profile where the time goes: for 30 seconds it records what the busy threads are doing and writes the busiest places to the log.

summary: Frame generation now also works for games that run slower than 15 fps.
changed: Frame generation keeps going for games below 15 frames per second and looks further for movement between two frames when the game is slow.

summary: Frame generation no longer makes the game wait for a free screen buffer.
fixed: Frame generation stalled the game while it waited for a free screen buffer; it now only adds a frame when one is free.

summary: The log now says what refresh rate the screen really runs at while a game is held at its top rate.
changed: The log records the screen's real refresh rate every few seconds when the screen is held at its top rate.

summary: Frame generation can be switched on and off from the in-game menu.
added: The in-game menu's Performance tab has a Frame generation switch, so you can turn it on and off while you play and compare.

summary: Frame generation no longer stalls the game, and reports what it does.
changed: Frame generation holds the screen at its top refresh rate and only generates a picture when the screen can show two per game frame (a game at 60 FPS or less on a 120 Hz screen). Faster games, or a moment when the screen has no free picture, are shown as they are.
With frame generation on, the log reports every two seconds how many pictures were generated, why others were not, and how long the screen kept the engine waiting.
fixed: Frame generation waited for a second picture from the screen on every frame, which could halve the game's speed and add a lot of input delay.

summary: Guides now show a drawing of the screen, and more screens have one.
added: Each guide step shows a small drawing of the screen it talks about, with the part to use ringed.
Some steps have a button that takes you there: add a game, open Steam, open the Play settings, open Stores and JIT.
Add a game explains its three ways in the first time it opens.
The first time the in-game menu opens, a short tip at the top explains its three tabs.
Settings, App, Tips and guides can play the how-to-play tour again, and open every guide.

summary: The first-game tour now comes before the game starts.
changed: The tour shown the first time you start a game is now a screen of its own before the game starts, with a picture of where the pencil and keyboard button will be, instead of a layer over the game. The game starts when the tour ends.
fixed: The tour's Next button no longer answers late: it was drawn over the game while the game was still starting.

summary: Tips: short guides explain each screen, and a short tour shows how to play.
added: Each screen (Home, Stores, Reports, Settings and a game's page) explains itself the first time you open it, in a few short steps. The question mark at the top of every screen opens that explanation again.
The first time you start any game, a short tour lights up the pencil and the keyboard button, shows the swipe in from the right edge that opens the menu, and explains how touching the game works.
Settings, App, Tips and guides turns tips off, shows them all again, or opens any guide.
changed: The one-line hint about the menu swipe is now part of the first-game tour. Installs that already had Porthole start with every tip marked as seen.

summary: All text encoding tables are included (Japanese, Chinese, Korean and others).
added: The text encoding tables for the Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Thai, Central European, Cyrillic, Greek, Turkish, Hebrew, Arabic, Baltic and Vietnamese code pages (and the other ones Wine provides) are now included. Programs that ask for a language setting such as "Japanese" no longer fail to create it.

summary: Log: the unhandled C++ exception report no longer disturbs the program.
changed: The extra text the log collects when a program stops with an unhandled C++ exception is now read only from memory that is certainly there. The previous build could end the program with a different error code while doing it.

summary: Log: more detail when a program stops with an unhandled C++ exception.
changed: The log of an unhandled C++ exception now also lists the text found on the stack at that moment, which usually includes the name that the failing call was given. Nothing else changes.

summary: Text encoding table for the Mac Roman code page; locale failures are named in the log.
added: The Mac Roman text encoding (code page 10000) is now included, so programs that ask for it no longer fail to find it.
changed: When a program asks for a language setting that cannot be created, the log now says which one.

summary: Log: the thrown error of a program that stops with an unhandled C++ exception is now named.
changed: When a program ends because of an unhandled C++ exception from Microsoft's runtime, the log now names the exception type and shows its message, so the cause can be found. Nothing else changes.

summary: Engine: web-based programs, step four.
changed: With pa-pool32-soft = 1 in a game's config, the placement of very large programs goes back to the module range, and one memory-layout assertion in the browser engine of one particular program build is skipped, since iOS has no address that could satisfy it. Nothing changes without that setting.

summary: Engine: very large programs are placed below 4 GB.
changed: With pa-pool32-soft = 1 in a game's config, a program of 128 MB or more that cannot have its preferred address is now placed below 4 GB, together with the memory block its browser engine uses for generated code, which that engine requires to be outside a region it reserves for itself. Replaces the previous placement. Nothing changes without that setting.

summary: Engine: very large programs are placed where their code memory has room.
changed: With pa-pool32-soft = 1 in a game's config, a program of 128 MB or more that cannot have its preferred address is now placed in the free stretch at the bottom of the module range, so that the 512 MB block its browser engine wants for generated code can sit in the same 4 GB region. Nothing changes without that setting.

summary: Engine: code memory for web-based programs is placed next to the program.
changed: With pa-pool32-soft = 1 in a game's config, the 512 MB block that the browser engine inside some programs wants for generated code is now looked for in the same 4 GB region as the program itself, which is where the engine insists on it. Nothing changes without that setting.

summary: Engine: more detail in the log about mid-size memory reservations.
changed: With pa-pool32-soft = 1 in a game's config, the memory-reservation log lines now also cover reservations of 256 MB to 1 GB. Nothing else changes.

summary: Engine: address-space reservations for web-based programs, step two.
changed: With pa-pool32-soft = 1 in a game's config, large address-space requests that the browser engine inside some programs makes are now answered inside the range it insists on, instead of being refused and retried. Nothing changes without that setting.

summary: Engine: more detail in the log about very large memory reservations.
changed: With pa-pool32-soft = 1 in a game's config, the memory-reservation log lines now also show a few registers and the data they point to. Nothing else changes.

summary: Engine: the memory-reservation log can now name the calling code.
changed: With pa-pool32-soft = 1 in a game's config, the log lines that name the code asking for and releasing huge address-space reservations now read the guest stack correctly (the first version printed nothing). Nothing else changes.

summary: Engine: more detail in the log about very large memory reservations.
changed: When a game's own config has pa-pool32-soft = 1, the log now names the code that asks for and gives back the biggest address-space reservations. Nothing else changes; it is there to find out why some programs still stop at start.

summary: Porthole installs on iOS 18 again.
changed: The minimum iOS version is 18 again (it was 26 for a few builds). It is developed and tested on iOS 26 and 27; iOS 18 to 25 should work but have not been tested. In-app JIT still needs iOS 18 or later, and creating a pairing file on the device still needs iOS 27 or later.

summary: The frame generation setting now says plainly that it can lower FPS and add input lag.
changed: Frame generation (experimental) on a game's Engine page now explains that it adds input delay and can lower the FPS of a game that already runs well (Factorio went from a steady 60 FPS to about 30 with a lot of lag). It stays off by default.

summary: Fixes the performance overlay being cut off at the top when you switch on more numbers while it is showing.
fixed: The performance overlay could be pushed up past the top of the screen, hiding its first rows, when more numbers or the graph were switched on while it was showing: the view that holds it kept its old size. It now fills the free part of the screen and the overlay sits in its corner inside that, so it can grow or shrink freely and always stays on screen.

summary: On small screens the performance overlay is shorter and wider, so more of the game stays visible.
changed: The performance overlay's list of numbers now takes at most about half the screen height and wraps into more columns beyond that, instead of a tall strip down the side. On phones with small screens this leaves much more of the game visible.

summary: The performance overlay no longer gets cut off when many numbers are on.
fixed: With many numbers, the graph or the developer details switched on, the performance overlay could run off the screen. The numbers now wrap into more columns when the height runs out, the developer details sit in their own column beside them, and if that is still too big the whole overlay shrinks to fit the screen from its corner.

summary: JIT and updates now work on cellular data: Porthole switches cellular data off for a moment and back on.
added: On cellular data (no Wi-Fi), enabling JIT or installing an update on this device asks to switch cellular data off for a few seconds, does it with a Shortcut, and switches it back on as soon as the job is done: after JIT is set up and before the game starts, or when the app restarts after an update. The private connection does not work while cellular data is in use, and neither job needs the internet. The tunnel comes up first, then cellular data goes off.

Two small Shortcuts are bundled (Porthole Cellular Off and Porthole Cellular On). The first time, Porthole offers to add them through the share sheet. Settings > JIT and tunnel > Cellular data has the same button, a test that switches cellular data off and straight back on once, and a switch to turn the feature off.
If cellular data could not be switched back on, the Home screen shows a notice with a Turn on button, and Porthole tries again whenever it opens.

summary: The pencil and keyboard buttons fade out so they are less visible.
changed: The pencil and keyboard buttons at the top left now fade with the edge handle: bright for a few seconds when a game starts or the menu closes, then faint. They light up when touched and keep working while faint. Menu > Game > Edge handle and quick buttons: Always visible keeps them bright.

summary: The in-game menu opens with a swipe in from the right edge; the Menu button is gone.
added: Swipe in from the right edge of the screen to open the in-game menu, and swipe the menu back to the right to close it. A thin handle on that edge shows for a few seconds when a game starts, then fades to a faint line. A tap on it opens the menu too. Choose how visible it is under Menu > Game > Opening this menu: Fades out, Always visible, or Hidden. The first time a game runs, a short hint says how to open the menu.
Touches that start in the 28-point strip at the right edge no longer reach the game.
changed: The labelled Menu button is removed from the top-left. The pencil and keyboard buttons stay.

summary: A new in-game menu: a side panel with Performance, Controls and Game tabs, and a performance overlay you can switch on.
added: The in-game menu is now a side panel that slides in over the game. Tabs: Performance (power mode for this game, Eco mode, GPU sync and the overlay settings), Controls (layout, show or hide the on-screen controls, look speed, the keyboard, bind sets and editing the controls) and Game (report how it runs, the touch controls guide, capture the next frame, close the game).

A performance overlay that is off until you turn it on in the menu. Pick the numbers (FPS, 1% low, frame time, CPU, busiest thread, GPU busy and frame time, memory, free memory, GPU memory, heat, battery, power mode, swap file), the corner, the size, the background, a one-line or list layout, and an optional frame graph. It never takes touches.
changed: The stats chip next to the Menu button is gone; the overlay replaces it. The on-screen controls and their editor are unchanged.

summary: Removes the Settings > Test page.
changed: The Settings > Test page (0.50.291 to 0.50.294) is gone, with the switches it added. Nothing else changes.

summary: Settings > Test: an optional switch to keep Valve's client's saved sign-in.
added: Keep Steam's saved sign-in, on the Test page (off by default). Porthole removes the login Valve's client saves each time the app starts and after a Steam session; with this on it leaves it alone so a login you made yourself stays.

summary: Settings > Test: a switch that freezes the Windows clock, as the old Madeira build did.
added: A switch on the Test page, Freeze the Windows clock, that runs Steam with GetTickCount held at zero (MADEIRA_USD_TIME=0), set early enough for the engine to read it. For comparing against the old build.

summary: Settings > Test: Steam launch options, engine lines, and a start that matches Madeira's own Steam Testing.
added: Two boxes on the Test page: extra Steam launch options, and engine lines in madeira.cfg's syntax (used for that test run only, like a game's own config). A button adds env.MADEIRA_JITLESS = 0, which lets Steam's web view use JIT instead of running interpreted. Both boxes are remembered. A switch, Start it Madeira's way, starts Steam the way Madeira's own Steam Testing button does (Wine's explorer shell on a desktop, the 64-bit cmd, Steam's -console flag) to compare against the normal start.

summary: Settings > Test: start your own Steam client, and Steam Big Picture, in a window.
added: A Test page in Settings. It looks for a copy of Steam in C:\\Steam (a folder named Steam on Wine's drive C:, next to Program Files) and starts steam.exe in a window on Wine's desktop with JIT switched on first, the way a game starts. A second button adds Big Picture mode. Nothing is saved in the library and a run leaves no compatibility prompt behind.

summary: Porthole now requires iOS 26 or later.
changed: The minimum iOS version is now 26 (it was 18, which Porthole was never tested on). iOS refuses to install this build on anything older, and the guide, website and docs say iOS 26 or later.

summary: The round Downloads button is solid, so it shows on light backgrounds.
changed: The Downloads button no longer shows the page through it: it has a solid background and a stronger edge.

summary: The Downloads button is now a round button at the bottom right of the Stores tab.
added: A round Downloads button that stays at the bottom right of the Stores tab, over every store's library and the games' pages, and does not move when you scroll or switch stores. A ring shows the progress of what is downloading and a number shows how many downloads there are.
changed: The Downloads buttons inside each store's row of controls are gone; the round button replaces them.

summary: One Downloads page for every store.
added: A single Downloads page that shows what Steam, Epic Games, GOG and itch.io are downloading, the games waiting, the paused or failed ones, and GOG or itch.io setups ready to install. Open it from the Downloads button in any store (it shows all stores' progress), from the Stores list, from All games, or from a Home download notice.
GOG and itch.io can now be paused, resumed, moved to the front (Download now) and removed from the Downloads page, like Steam and Epic.
changed: Steam and Epic no longer have a Downloads page of their own; Back returns to the store you came from.

summary: Setup now covers all four stores, says plainly what is sent, and has a Good to know page; Porthole warns you in a game when memory is nearly full.
added: A Good to know page at the end of setup: the first start is slower, big games may need Swap, controllers, and Performance mode up to 120 FPS.
A warning over the game when the swap file is nearly full or the device is nearly out of memory, saying what to change (at most four times a session).
changed: Setup's Games step and Add a game now offer GOG and itch.io as well as Steam, Epic Games and Files, and signing in to either counts as games added.
The privacy note in setup says exactly what Porthole sends and when.
Home shows GOG and itch.io downloads as well as Steam and Epic ones.

summary: Security: store sign-ins leave no copy in the network cache, picked certificates and pairing files are deleted after import, and updates are checked against the maintainer's signature.
changed: Epic, GOG and itch.io (and Steam's cloud saves) now use a connection that keeps nothing on disk: no cache, no cookies. Before, iOS's shared cache could hold their tokens and API key, and a Windows program in the app could read them. The old cache is emptied once.

A pairing file, certificate or profile you pick is deleted from the app's temporary folder as soon as it has been read (it is kept in the Keychain); leftovers from earlier versions are removed at start.
Updates are installed only when they carry the maintainer's signature (builds that carry the release key; the download is also checked against the signed checksum).
Steam cloud saves are always downloaded over https.
Problem reports also hide public IPv6 addresses and any password, token or API key that appears next to its name. The pairing log no longer names your iPhone.
Pairing from this iPhone's Settings stops after five wrong codes.

summary: Security hardening: logins and keys are kept where Windows programs cannot read them.
changed: The pairing file (the key that lets a computer debug this iPhone) is now kept in the Keychain instead of a file in the app's storage, and is moved there on first start.

Update certificates, their passwords and this install's report key are kept in the Keychain only; a fallback file that an earlier version could leave in the app's storage is moved into the Keychain and deleted.

After each Steam session, and when the app starts, the sign-in tokens and account names that Valve's own client saves inside Porthole are removed, and those folders are kept out of device backups. Porthole signs Steam in again for every game anyway.
Problem reports also hide GOG and itch.io account names, Steam 64-bit ids, and Epic account ids and names that appear on a game's command line.
Epic's sign-in page no longer keeps cookies, and Sign out clears any an earlier version kept.
The update server address must be https (plain http is accepted only for this device itself).

summary: Free games from your itch.io collections are listed too.
changed: Stores > itch.io: games in your itch.io collections that are free (including pay-what-you-want at zero) and have a Windows download are now listed next to the games you bought or claimed, and install the same way. Refresh the list to see them.

summary: itch.io's own icon in the Stores tab.
changed: Stores: the itch.io store now shows itch.io's real storefront icon instead of a drawn tile.

summary: itch.io joins the Stores tab.
added: Stores: itch.io is a fourth store. Sign in with a personal API key (made on itch.io's API keys page, which opens inside Porthole), and the games you bought, claimed or got in bundles that have a Windows download are listed with their covers. Open a game, pick which download to use if there are several, and tap Install: Porthole downloads the file (pause and resume, download card and Live Activity like the other stores), unpacks the zip, finds the game's program and adds it to your library. Single-exe games work too, and installers (an .exe named setup or an .msi) run on the Wine desktop and are picked up afterwards. Browser-only games are not listed, and 7z or rar downloads are not supported yet.

summary: GOG pictures are no longer washed out.
fixed: Stores > GOG: the pictures looked pale and faded to white at the bottom, because they were GOG's store-page background. They are now GOG's own card picture of each game (the one with the title), which is clean and full colour.

summary: GOG games whose program name differs in capitals now finish installing.
fixed: GOG: RollerCoaster Tycoon Deluxe and other games stopped at The installer finished but RCT.exe is not there, because GOG's info file spells the program RCT.exe and the download holds RCT.EXE, and this file system is case-sensitive. The program is now found whatever its capitals. Press Try again on such a game; the files are already there.

summary: GOG games now download straight from GOG, no setup program needed.
added: Stores > GOG: a game that GOG has a Galaxy build of (Fallout 2 and most of the catalogue) is downloaded straight from GOG's servers: Porthole reads the build's file list, fetches the pieces in parallel, checks every piece and file against GOG's checksums and writes the game into C:\\GOG. There is no setup program to run, so it is faster and does not depend on Wine running GOG's installer. Games without a Galaxy build still use GOG's setup file.
fixed: GOG: the setup-file route stopped with a path not found popup for Fallout 2 on the Wine desktop (the setup read a damaged file path while loading shell32). Fallout 2 no longer uses it.

summary: GOG installs no longer fail with a wrong-size error.
fixed: GOG: every game stopped at A downloaded file was the wrong size even though the whole file had arrived, because GOG lists file sizes rounded to whole megabytes. The download is now checked against the size the server states and GOG's own checksum.

summary: Install GOG games: Porthole downloads GOG's setup file and runs it for you.
added: Stores > GOG: open a game and tap Install. Porthole downloads GOG's own setup file (with pause, resume and a checksum check, and the download card and Live Activity like Steam and Epic), runs it silently inside Wine into C:\\GOG, then adds the game to your library with the right program, and deletes the setup files. This is the route for older GOG games that have no download of their own, such as Fallout 2. Games installed this way can be uninstalled from the game's sheet or from Settings > Storage.

summary: GOG's own icon in the Stores tab.
changed: Stores: the GOG store now shows GOG's real icon instead of a drawn tile, and the search box says 1 game rather than 1 games.

summary: GOG joins the Stores tab: sign in and see your library.
added: Stores: GOG is a third store next to Steam and Epic Games. Sign in on GOG's own page and the games you own that have a Windows version are listed, with their pictures, search and a badge in All games. Downloading and installing from GOG is the next step, so for now each game only opens a page with a link to it on GOG.

summary: See everything that changed since the version you have.
added: Settings > Updates: tap Update available (under Check for updates) to see the New, Changed and Fixed lists of every version since the one you have, each line tagged with its version, plus a one-line summary of each version and the update button at the bottom.

summary: Calmer with no connection.
added: Steam, Epic Games and All games show an Offline chip when the device has no network, and keep showing the saved list.
changed: With no network, refreshing the Steam or Epic library, the compatibility list and the answers to your problem reports waits quietly instead of failing with a red error; they refresh when the connection is back.
Settings > Updates says Offline instead of a failed check, and the Reports lists say the list needs a connection.
A Steam library refresh that works clears an old error.

summary: Home tells you when a Steam game you have installed has an update.
added: Home shows a notice when a Steam game on the device has a newer build on Steam (Factorio has an update, or 3 Steam games have updates, with their names). Tapping it opens the Steam library, where the games with an update carry the Update badge. It comes back when another game, or a newer build of the same one, appears.
changed: Porthole looks for new Steam builds each time you come back to it when its list is over six hours old, not only when it starts.

summary: Home tells you when a report was answered, and My reports is at the top.
added: When the maintainer reviews or fixes a report you sent, or adds a note, Home shows a notice (Your report was fixed in 0.50.xxx, or was reviewed, with the note). Tapping it opens Report a problem. Porthole looks for answers when it opens and when you come back to it.
changed: Report a problem: My reports is the first thing on the page, above the form to send a new one.

summary: A crash report now carries the right run first.
fixed: After a game ended unexpectedly, the part of a report labelled as the run that ended could be the run before it (the log was read before this launch had set the finished run's log aside). It is now the run that ended, and the game's own log is added only when it is a different file.

summary: A problem report carries the whole log of the run, not a slice of it.
changed: Report a problem now includes the whole log of the run that is reported (and of the run before it, or, after a crash, of the run that ended and the game's own log), cleaned of personal parts. A report sent to the server is packed first (a log shrinks about ten to one), so a 25 MB log travels as a few megabytes. A log over 60 MB keeps its first 2 MB and its last part and says what it left out. The preview row shows the start and the end and says how much is between.

summary: A report after a crash carries the crashed run, not the launch that followed it.
added: When Porthole opens and finds that the last run ended while a game was running (a crash, iOS closing the app, or a force-quit), it keeps that run's log and the game's own log aside, three at a time. Settings > Report a problem then offers to include the crash (on by default), and a report uses the crashed run's log first, then the game's own log if it is a different file, then a little of the launch after it, so opening the app again, even twice, no longer loses the crash. The Report a problem page shows a ! until such a crash has been reported.
changed: A sent report's upload makes room for the crashed run (about 1 MB of its end).

summary: Tap a report to read the maintainer's whole answer.
changed: Settings > Report a problem > My reports: tapping a report opens it, with its status, the whole note from the maintainer, what you sent and when it was answered. Withdrawing a report is a button inside it, so a tap on the list no longer asks to withdraw.

summary: Send a problem to Porthole's server and follow what happens to it.
added: Settings > Report a problem > Send it to Porthole's server: the report (what you wrote, the facts about the install and, if you leave the switch on, the cleaned end of the log) goes to the maintainer, privately. Under My reports you see each one as Open, Reviewed or Fixed in a version, with a note from the maintainer, and a number on the Settings page when something was answered. You can withdraw a report. Nothing is sent without that button and a confirmation, and what would be sent is what the preview row shows.
