summary: Report a problem has its own page in Settings.
changed: Report a problem is a page of its own in the Settings list, after Advanced, instead of a row inside About and Log.

summary: Report a problem: a file with what is needed, and nothing sent without you.
added: Settings > App > About, and Settings > Advanced > Log: Report a problem. Describe it in a sentence, look at exactly what would be shared, then save or share the file (Files, AirDrop, Discord, mail), open an issue on GitHub or ask on Discord. The file has the app and engine version, the device and iOS, how it was installed, and the end of this run's log and the one before, with the app's folder names, your account names, e-mail addresses and public IP addresses taken out. Nothing is sent by the app.

summary: Epic games start without a connection.
changed: Starting an Epic game with no connection (airplane mode, or Epic out of reach for more than ten seconds) no longer fails: the game starts without Epic's sign-in, like Epic's own offline mode. A single-player game just runs; one that needs Epic's online services will say it cannot reach them. If Epic answers but refuses, the error is shown as before.

summary: Epic updates, a Storage page, sorting in the stores and a lighter background.
added: Epic Games: an installed game with a newer build on Epic shows "Update" on its tile and page. Updating downloads only the files that differ, into the same folder; cancelling an update keeps the game installed.
Settings > Storage: free space, every game with its size (biggest first), a way to delete a Steam or Epic game's files, and a button to clear temporary files.
Stores: a sort button in the Steam, Epic and All games grids (A to Z, Recently played, Installed first, Largest first for Steam). The choice is kept.
Epic: a read-only check of the game's cloud saves is written to the log when you start an Epic game (counts only), so that syncing them can be built on the real answer.
changed: The moving background rests while a list is being scrolled.
Reports builds its list as you scroll, and a big Home shelf (more than 24 games) does too.
Home shows an Epic download in its notices like a Steam one, and tapping it opens the Epic downloads.

summary: Settings pages look like buttons.
changed: Settings: each page (Play, Stores and JIT, Saves, Updates, App, Advanced) is a card with an outline, a bigger icon and an arrow, so it reads as a button instead of words in a list.

summary: Tap a version in Updates to read what changed before installing it.
added: Settings > Updates > Versions: tapping a version opens a page with its summary and what it added, changed and fixed, with the install button at the bottom. Before, it went straight to an install question.
changed: Going back to an older version shows its warning on that page, above the button, instead of in a separate question.

summary: The setup guide fits a phone held sideways.
changed: Setup guide, phone held sideways: Back, the main button and a round close button sit in the top row beside the three steps, so every page gets the whole height instead of being cut off by a bar of buttons at the bottom. The welcome and final pages put their picture beside the title.

summary: Settings: the Epic Games block no longer duplicates the library.
changed: Settings > Stores and JIT > Epic Games: "Your Epic games" is a plain count now, not a button that jumps to the library. The library is in the Stores tab.

summary: The update popup asks about pausing your VPN itself.
changed: When another VPN is on while the app updates itself, the "Pause your VPN?" question appears inside the update popup (Pause it / Keep it on) instead of in a window of its own, with the progress and the keep-the-app-open warning in view. Other installs and starting a game keep the separate question.

summary: The setup guide and Add a game offer Epic Games next to Steam.
added: Setup guide, step 3: an Epic Games section next to Steam and Files. It shows whether you are signed in and opens the Epic sign-in; the last page lists Epic Games with the other sources.
Add a game: Download from Epic Games, next to Download from Steam.
changed: The step counts as done when you are signed in to Steam or Epic Games, or have imported a game.
The Windows installer row says GOG or a disc: Epic games now have their own download.

summary: Signing the app is several times faster.
changed: Signing (on this device, with your certificate) spent most of its time packing the IPA again: every file's checksum was worked out one byte at a time and every file was compressed again. Files signing does not change are now written back as they were, checksums are eight bytes at a time, and the rest is compressed on all cores. On a Mac the same build went from 10.4 s to 2.0 s; the result passes codesign and zip's own check.

summary: Faster "Sending to the installer" step when the app updates itself.
changed: The signed build is copied to the device's installer over four connections at once instead of one, which waited for an answer after every 64 KB. If anything goes wrong with that, it copies over one connection as before. The log says which way was used and how long it took.

summary: The update popup blurs the page behind it.
changed: Behind the update popup the page is blurred and dimmed instead of just darkened; the card itself stays solid.

summary: The update popup is solid.
changed: The popup shown while the app updates itself has a solid card and a darker backdrop, so the page behind it no longer shows through the text.

summary: Updating the app from inside it now takes over the screen with the progress and a warning to stay.
added: While Porthole updates itself with your certificate, a full-screen popup shows the steps (Download, Sign, Install), one progress bar for the whole trip with the percentage, and a clear warning to keep the app open and on that screen: no closing it, no switching apps, no locking the phone. Nothing underneath can be pressed meanwhile, and the screen stays awake. It ends with the result and a Close button; there is also a Cancel the update button.

summary: Much less lag in the Stores tab and while downloading.
changed: The Steam, Epic and All games grids only build the tiles on (and just beside) the screen, so a library of hundreds scrolls smoothly. Before, every game was drawn and watched at once.

Download progress reaches the screens once a second (Steam) or twice a second (Epic) instead of hundreds of times a second for Epic, and an installed game's state is looked up on disk every half minute instead of every five seconds.

Unpacking and checking downloaded pieces runs at a lower priority than the screen, so scrolling keeps its frames while a download runs. All games builds and sorts its list once per redraw instead of several times.
A tile that scrolls out of sight by touch no longer passes the glow to another tile.

summary: A live download card on the lock screen and in the Dynamic Island, with Pause, Resume and Cancel.
added: Downloads (Steam and Epic) show a Live Activity: the game, percentage, size, speed and time left on the lock screen and in the Dynamic Island, with Pause / Resume and Cancel buttons you can press without opening the app. When a download finishes the card says it is ready to play; a paused queue keeps its Resume button for 15 minutes.

New optional extension F4Activity (site.portholehq.app.activity) draws the card. Like the tunnel and the JIT helper it can be removed while signing to spend one App ID less; the download card of iOS (percentage, size, speed) is used then. The Complete install is now four App IDs.
changed: Settings > Your install counts the App IDs this copy uses and says whether the download card is inside.

summary: The download card shows the percentage, size, speed and time left.
added: Epic Games downloads get the same iOS download card Steam's have (lock screen and Dynamic Island), with a progress bar and a stop control.
changed: The download card now reads, for example, 42% · 1.3 GB of 3.1 GB · 18 MB/s · 7 min left · +2 waiting, updated every second, under the game's name and a progress bar.

summary: Downloads keep going at full speed after you leave the app.
changed: Steam and Epic downloads now hold the app awake with silent audio (the app's audio background mode, like on-device pairing) for as long as something is downloading, and let go when the queue is empty. iOS no longer throttles the download to a crawl once the app is left, and Epic downloads no longer pause after half a minute. Nothing is played; the silence does not interrupt your music.
fixed: Downloads stalled or crawled at a very low speed once the app was swiped away from, with only the download card showing.

summary: Compatibility badges are back on the Steam and Epic libraries.
fixed: The compatibility badge (Worked / Somewhat worked / Didn't work / Not yet tested, or what it did on an older engine) is back in the corner of every Steam and Epic game, in the grids and on the all-games page. It sits under the download or installed badge. An Epic game gets its badge once it is installed, because reports are matched to the installed program.

summary: Stores: no empty bar above the library.
changed: The store icons (Steam, Epic Games, All games) now sit in the same row as the refresh and Downloads buttons instead of a bar of their own, so the games start higher on the screen. The search box and filters follow directly under them.

summary: Swipe in from the left edge to go back.
added: Swiping in from the left edge goes back, as in any iOS app: out of a game's page, a store's game page, the Downloads page, a Settings page and the rest. It does what the B button does on a controller.

summary: The Stores button is gone from the store pages.
changed: Inside Steam, Epic Games or All games the "Stores" button is gone; the store icons at the top right already take you to another store, and the Stores tab still opens the list.

summary: Epic Games looks and works like Steam: a grid, a Downloads page and a page for every game.
added: Epic Games: a Downloads page with the running download, its speed and time left, the queue (with Download now and Remove) and the paused ones, plus Pause all and Resume all.

Epic Games: every game has its own page, like Steam's: the picture, the developer, the description and screenshots where Epic has them, Install / Pause / Resume / Play / Game settings, how it runs on Porthole, and Details and files (version, delete files).
A game's page opens from the all-games grid too, whichever store it is from.
changed: Epic's library is a grid of pictures with a badge for what each game is doing (percent, waiting, paused, installed), a search box, an All / Installed filter and a refresh button, the same as Steam's.
All games is a grid now too, with the store's logo in the corner of each picture.

summary: Settings rows press anywhere, and the game page header no longer scrolls.
changed: A game's page held sideways on a phone: the back button, the name and Play share the top row and the chips sit in a short row under it. They wrap instead of scrolling, so every one is always in view.
fixed: Settings: the page list on the left (and the tabs in the top bar, the pill buttons and the Home notices) could only be pressed on their words. The whole row or button answers a press now.

summary: Cleaner top bar, and a game page that uses a phone's landscape height.
changed: The tab in the top bar is marked by its highlight and bolder name only; the line under it is gone.
A game's page held sideways on a phone: the back button, the name, the chips and Play now share one row, and the settings below get the room (tighter spacing too), so more of them fit at once.

summary: Home fixes: store badge placement, one Steam badge, Settings reachable in landscape.
changed: The top bar no longer shows the JIT and tunnel status chips, so Settings is not pushed off the bar on a phone held sideways. JIT is still reported where it matters (the Home notices and Settings).
fixed: The store badge on a game tile no longer covers the compatibility badge: it moved to the bottom corner.
A Steam game showed two Steam badges in its details; it shows one now (and "Direct" only for a game run without Steam).

summary: The Settings page that held Steam is now called Stores and JIT.
changed: Settings > Steam and JIT is now Stores and JIT, since it holds Steam, Epic Games and the SSD game storage as well as the JIT connection.

summary: The store badges are the launchers' real logos.
changed: The Stores tab, the cards on Home and the game pages show the real Steam and Epic Games logos instead of drawn stand-ins (on a light round backing so the dark Epic shield stays visible).

summary: A Stores tab: Steam, Epic Games and all your games in one place, with a badge showing where each came from.
added: The Steam tab is now Stores. It lists each launcher (Steam, Epic Games) with how many games you have there and how many are installed; tap one to open its library, or open All games to see every launcher's games on one page. A row of buttons on top jumps between launchers and All games.
Epic Games has its own library page: sign in, search, install, pause, resume, cancel, play and uninstall right there.
A small badge for the store a game came from sits on the picture of its card on Home, on the game's page and in the all-games list. New launchers will appear in the same tab.
changed: Settings > Stores and JIT > Epic Games now opens the Epic library in the Stores tab. Epic games use Epic's own artwork on Home.

summary: Steam games on an external SSD, and Epic Games.
added: Settings > Stores and JIT > Game storage: choose a folder on an SSD plugged into the device and send new Steam downloads there. The game's files, download progress and caches stay on the SSD; Windows and Steam's client files stay on the device. Check the connection or select the folder again after unplugging.

Settings > Stores and JIT > Epic Games: sign in on Epic's own page, see the games your account owns that have a Windows version, install them straight from Epic (resume, pause, cancel, uninstall) and play them without Epic's launcher. Epic's overlay, anti-cheat and other launchers are not supported.
changed: Steam games started through Valve's client now find their install folder on the SSD (E: and C:\MadeiraExternalLibrary), registered as a Steam library.
Unpacking the prefix refuses names with '..'; command lines with passwords or tokens are not logged.

summary: Engine update: ten open Madeira fixes, the x87 switch works, more of Windows' own libraries.
added: Game details > Engine: Large memory reservations (for Final Fantasy Tactics - The Ivalice Chronicles, which reserves 256 GB at start).

The 64-bit library set now includes the versioned DirectX helpers many older and Unreal games ask for by exact name (D3DX9 24-42, D3DX10 33-43, D3DCompiler 33-47, XAudio2 0-9, X3DAudio, XAPOFX, Direct3D 10), tbs.dll, and Windows' WMA decoder.
changed: Reduced-precision x87 'Off' now really turns it off. Before, it only removed the setting, and the engine's own default for 32-bit games is On (this is what stopped the character moving in Assassin's Creed).

Engine: a program that starts a second copy of itself (a launcher) can now start it; Chromium-style programs with several processes keep their thread-local slots apart; decommitting memory that was never committed no longer kills the thread; the stuck-fault breaker counts per thread.

Engine: a store that crosses a 16 KB page of an aliased range is split per page (low-memory iPads), Direct3D 12 command list 8, an empty pipeline library and a view-list lock were added for Final Fantasy Tactics and other Direct3D 12 games.
Desktop mouse look: the cursor's visibility follows the program, so a USB mouse no longer accelerates near the screen edges or snaps on a click.
The window the game shows first (often a splash) no longer hides the real window: windows first shown minimized after the starting screen are still restored.
Prefix archives reject names with '..' and bad size fields. DXMT's memory census report runs once every 10 seconds (it filled a third of the log).
fixed: Credential-like values on a program's command line are no longer written to the log.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: the browser engine's second 16 GB reserve is served without backing.
changed: Engine (Red Dead Redemption 2 only): the previous build got the browser engine past its 1 GB tables; it then asked for another 16 GB reserve that needs a 16 GB boundary, and every free hole was used up. That ask is now served as an unbacked range at an unused aligned address; memory is only mapped when the engine writes to it. Not verified on a device.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: the browser engine's aligned 1 GB reserves finally have somewhere to go.
changed: Engine (Red Dead Redemption 2 only): the browser engine's 1 GB and 4 GB reserves must sit on a 4 GB boundary, and the address space has no such free spot left. They are now placed at fixed aligned spots in the middle of a 32 GB range whose owner only uses its first megabytes. Not verified on a device.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: the browser engine's 1 GB aligned reserves are served.
added: When the helper process ends with an error the log now lists its last memory calls.
changed: Engine (Red Dead Redemption 2 only): the browser engine asks for 1 GB reserves that must sit on a 4 GB boundary. The previous build handed out unaligned ranges three times, found no room for the longer retry and ended with an out-of-memory error. They now get an aligned range in the largest free hole. Not verified on a device.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: the browser engine's reserve is no longer given up after a large decommit.
changed: Engine (Red Dead Redemption 2 only): the previous build served the browser engine's 16 GB reserve, but the engine then released the first 4 GB of it, which was longer than the real memory behind it, and gave up. Releases and protection changes that run past the real part are now clipped to it, and 4 GB reserves are served the same way as the 16 GB ones. Not verified on a device.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: the browser engine's follow-up memory requests are served and no longer wipe the allocator's pages.
changed: Engine (Red Dead Redemption 2 only): in the previous build the browser engine got its sandbox and then asked again for 16 GB and 8 GB blocks; the repeated 8 GB answers released a range the memory allocator was already writing to, which crashed the helper. The range is now carved once and the later requests are served from free holes. Not verified on a device.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: the browser engine's smallest memory sandbox is served.
changed: Engine (Red Dead Redemption 2 only): the previous build got the browser engine past its first big reserve, then it asked for its memory sandbox (1.3 TB, halving to 8 GB) and every size was refused, which ends in an out-of-memory error. The 8 GB size is now served from the unused top of a 32 GB range that nothing has ever written to. Not verified on a device.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: the browser engine's memory sandbox no longer lands on the allocator's pool.
added: After a crash the log now lists the last memory calls the game made, so the next failure shows which one went wrong.
changed: Engine (Red Dead Redemption 2 only): Chromium's JavaScript engine asks for a 32 GB (then 16 GB) block aligned to 16 GB. In the last two builds that block was placed on the second half of the memory allocator's own pool, so both wrote the same pages. It now shares a second 32 GB range that nothing has ever used, or is refused if that is gone. Not verified on a device.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: the browser host's third 32 GB reserve no longer lands on top of the memory allocator's own pool.
changed: Engine (Red Dead Redemption 2 only): Rockstar's Chromium host asks for a third 32 GB range from its in-process renderer thread. It was answered with a range that sat exactly on the memory allocator's pool, so two allocators wrote the same pages and the host stopped on a corrupted allocator check. That ask now gets 2 GB of real memory on a 4 GB-aligned address in the biggest free hole. Not verified on a device.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: Oilpan's large pages get real memory; the log names the build.
added: The first lines of the log name the app version, build and engine, so a log can always be matched to the build that wrote it.
changed: Engine (Red Dead Redemption 2 only): Chromium's caged heap keeps its large objects in the upper half of its 32 GB reservation, which started inside the emulator's band; 2 GB there are now really reserved and the band starts above them. In the previous build the browser host got through all its thread creation and then stopped on exactly that commit. Not verified on a device.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: a 16 GB emulator band again.
changed: Engine (Red Dead Redemption 2 only): the emulator's address band is 16 GB again (it was 8 GB, which the Steam client alone filled), the 8 GB V8 holdback is not made, and the real part of a big random-address reserve is 1 GB instead of 4 GB. Rockstar's Chromium host got as far as creating over a hundred threads before the band ran out. Not verified on a device.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: a big random-address reserve gets a real start in the biggest hole.
changed: Engine (Red Dead Redemption 2 only): Rockstar's Chromium host now starts in one process and gets through its allocator setup; it then stopped on a commit inside the emulator's reserved band, after a 16 GB reserve at a random address was answered with an address across several reserved areas. Such a reserve is now placed in the largest free hole with its first part (up to 4 GB) really reserved. Not verified on a device.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: Chromium host runs single-process, Oilpan gets its slot.
changed: Engine (Red Dead Redemption 2 only): the JIT pool's RW alias moves above the first 4 GB of the top slot so Chromium's Oilpan heap can have it; Oilpan's reserve is no longer answered with an overlapping soft slot; and Rockstar's Chromium host (SocialClubHelper.exe) is started in single-process mode with its helper processes refused, because every process shares one address space and a second Chromium cannot get its own pools. The first helper now got its allocator pool in 0.50.220 and then stopped on the Oilpan reserve. Not verified on a device.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: room for Chromium's allocator in the launcher.
changed: Engine (opt-in, switched on for Red Dead Redemption 2 only): the emulator's address band moves out of the top 32 GB so Chromium's memory allocator can get the 32 GB-aligned pool it asks for. Rockstar's launcher showed that it timed out loading its content because its Chromium helper programs stopped at start for lack of that pool. Also available per game as the line pa-pool32-soft = 1. Not verified on a device.

summary: Rockstar launcher: programs that rewrite their own code keep the code copy.
changed: Engine: a plain x64 program with a section that is both executable and writable (Rockstar's Launcher.exe and RockstarService.exe, packed programs) keeps its copy in the code pool even when big x64 programs are kept out of it. The Red Dead Redemption 2 launcher chain reached Social Club in 0.50.218 and then ended in a storm of write faults on exactly those programs. Not verified on a device.

summary: Privacy: less leaves the device.
added: Settings > Advanced > Links: ask before a porthole:// link starts a game (on by default).
When an update could not be installed on the device, the signed file is kept and can be saved or shared from Settings > Updates.
changed: Compatibility badges: the app downloads the public list of badges and matches your games against it on the device. The server is no longer told which games you have.
The pairing file is kept in a private folder (it was in Documents, which the Files app shows). An existing one is moved there the first time it is needed.
Updating no longer has a server fallback: a signed copy of the app is never uploaded. It is signed and installed on the device.

summary: External display support is out again.
changed: The external display feature of 0.50.210 to 0.50.216 is removed and the app behaves as before it. AirPlay Screen Mirroring on an iPhone is only a copy of the screen, so the game could not be moved to the TV with the controls left on the device.

summary: The AirPlay mirror workaround is out.
added: The log records every scene iOS asks the app about (iOS asked for a scene configuration: role=...), so a cable connection can be told apart from AirPlay.
changed: Settings > Play > Display > Play on a connected display now says that a cable gives a real second screen and AirPlay Screen Mirroring on an iPhone is only a copy of the screen.
fixed: Removed the 0.50.214 'keep the controls out of a mirrored screen' option: it fought UIKit over the order of the views, hid the controls on the device as well and broke touching them afterwards.

summary: External display: scene setup copied from how Amethyst does it.
changed: The app delegate now answers for the external-display scene role and names its own scene delegate (the log says: the external scene delegate was called), as Amethyst does. 0.50.211 to 0.50.214 never got a display scene from iOS.

summary: AirPlay mirroring: the TV shows the game, the controls stay on the device.
added: While the screen is being mirrored with AirPlay (or recorded), the touch controls and menu are kept out of the mirrored picture, so the TV shows only the game and the controls stay on your iPhone or iPad. The TV shows the shape of your device's screen; a cable to a display still gives a full-screen picture. Settings > Play > Display > Keep the controls out of a mirrored screen turns it off.

summary: Display diagnostics: mirroring state and audio route.
added: The log also records whether the screen is being mirrored or captured, the audio output (AirPlay, HDMI) and whether the app's signed copy still has its scene manifest.

summary: More display diagnostics.
added: The log lists the screens and scenes iOS has given the app: at launch, when a screen connects, and when a game's screen opens.

summary: External display: connect the screen the way SwiftUI allows.
added: The log says what iOS did when a display was connected: [display] watching, scene connecting (role and size), external display connected.
fixed: A connected display only mirrored the device in 0.50.210 and the display code never ran: the app's SwiftUI shell answers for every scene, so the delegate named in Info.plist was never used. The display window is now made when iOS announces the display (UIScene.willConnectNotification).

summary: Play on a TV or monitor, with the controls on your device.
added: External display: connect a TV or monitor (AirPlay, or a USB-C / Lightning cable) and the game fills that screen while the touch controls, the menu and the controller pointer stay on your iPhone or iPad. Steam games (through Dock) follow too. Between games the display shows a waiting screen with the Porthole mark. Settings > Play > Display > Other screens turns it off, which hands the display back to normal mirroring.
The log has [display] lines for a connected display, so a bad start can be diagnosed.
changed: Releases are built in the Release configuration (the same source; compared against Debug on a device with no noticeable difference).

summary: Last played is saved while you play, and the restart after a game is explained.
added: After a game ends, Home shows a Close Porthole button (Restart to play another game) instead of leaving you to find the app switcher.
changed: The end-of-game message says what to do: close Porthole and open it again to play another game.
Pressing Play after a game has run in this session says that Porthole has to close first, instead of trying to start a second game in the same run.
fixed: Most recently played games now go to the front of the shelf even when the game closes the whole app: the last-played time is saved when a game starts and the play time once a minute, not only when the game ends cleanly.

summary: Release-configuration build (experiment).
changed: This build is compiled in the Release configuration instead of Debug: the app's own C code is optimised. It is the same source as 0.50.207. Release builds used to crash the guest; the cause (missing exported symbols) was fixed in the project, but this is the first one to be tried on a device. If a game that worked on 0.50.207 does not start, go back to 0.50.207 from Settings > Updates.

summary: Credits link to each project.
changed: Settings > App > About and credits: every project Porthole took inspiration from opens its GitHub page (Madeira, Iridium, StikDebug, idevice, StikPair and the OpenGL fork of Madeira). The credits file lists links for the upstream projects too.

summary: Install with fewer App IDs, and the app checks how it was signed.
added: One IPA can be installed three ways to spend fewer App IDs: complete (3 App IDs), without the tunnel extension (2; LocalDevVPN provides the private link), or without both extensions (1; StikDebug or another tool switches JIT on). Remove the extensions when you sign; the app notices what is missing and adapts.

Settings > Steam and JIT > Your install: shows which extensions are inside and whether the signature actually carries get-task-allow, Increased Memory Limit, Extended Virtual Addressing and the Network Extensions permission, with what to do about each one that is missing.
A notice on Home when the signature is missing a permission games need, and a signature that is about to expire.
The Launcher and the in-app updater can sign an update without chosen extensions (LauncherCore: SigningOptions.stripExtensionNames), so an update of a lighter install stays a lighter install.
changed: The setup guide no longer asks you to allow the private link when this install has no tunnel, and hides the in-app method when there is no JIT helper.
Without the tunnel extension, Play never pauses your own VPN (there is nothing of ours to start).

summary: Credits list projects, not people.
changed: The credits (Settings > App > About, the pairing screen and the credits file) name the projects Porthole is built on and no longer name individual people. The licence texts keep their own copyright lines.

summary: Reports need 5 minutes of play again.
changed: A game can be reported as working again only after 5 minutes of play (the test change in 0.50.203 is taken out).

summary: Test build: reports can be sent without the 5 minutes of play.
changed: TEMPORARY, for testing: a game can be reported as working without playing it for 5 minutes. The server has to allow it too. This is taken out again when the testing is done.

summary: Hide the notices at the top of Home with a small x.
added: The chips at the top of Home (report a game, update ready, Windows components, a finished installer, finish setting up) have a small x that hides them. The x on the question about how a game ran dismisses the question; hiding Update ready only hides that version, so a newer update shows again.

summary: An app icon: a silver porthole looking at a sunset sea, a night sky in dark mode. The porthole is in the top bar too.
added: The app has an icon: a silver porthole with a cyan sea, a small island with a palm and a sunset. In dark mode it is a night sky with a crescent moon and a shooting star; tinted icons get a grey version.
The same porthole sits next to the app's name in the top bar (the name shows on iPad and wide phones).

summary: A look closer to Steam's: slate-blue surfaces, with Porthole's own light on top.
changed: The default colour scheme (Deep Sea) moves to Steam-like slate blue with cooler panels and softer text, a diagonal background, and a calmer glow; the cyan-to-violet accent and the porthole ring stay Porthole's own. Other colour schemes keep their colours and share the new panels and text.

summary: Home with a controller: the chosen game is wide, the others step back.
changed: While a controller is connected, the game row on Home works like Steam's Big Picture shelf: the chosen game's tile grows wide and the others shrink, with the change animated as you move along. With touch only, every tile stays the same size.

summary: Tap the controller badge on a game's page to see what it means.
added: On a game's page (library and Steam), pressing the controller badge explains what full or partial controller support means, and for partial, how to cover the parts a controller cannot reach.

summary: Controller badges: full and partial look different.
changed: Full controller support is a solid green badge reading FULL; partial is an amber, dashed-outline badge reading PARTIAL. On a game's page they spell out Full controller support or Partial controller support.

summary: Updates without a certificate: download the file, with a link to GitHub.
added: With no certificate added, Settings > Updates offers each version (the newest and older ones) as a plain download: the file is fetched as published, unsigned, and handed to the share sheet (Save to Files, AirDrop). A note and a button link to the releases on GitHub.
changed: The "Needs signing" dead end is gone: the Update button becomes Download when there is nothing to sign with. People who have added a certificate and a profile still update from inside the app as before.

summary: Setup guide: three steps instead of five.
changed: The setup guide is Full speed (the pairing file and the private link on one page), Windows components, and Games. The automatic JIT method is chosen for you, with "Use a different method" a tap away.
Signing certificates and profiles left the setup guide: they are in Settings > Updates, with a "What is this?" explanation, for people who want the app to update itself.

summary: Reports: a short list, and the details only when you ask for them.
added: On a game's reports, "Show the details" adds the settings that worked, the per-device results and the iOS / app / files-source lines of each report.
changed: The Reports list: one sort switch (Most reports / A to Z), no icon on every row.
A game's reports show the verdict, then each report as device, date, how it ran and the comment. The rest is behind Show the details.

summary: Downloads: plain words instead of rows of small icons.
changed: Downloads: the four chips became one line ("2 in the queue · 4 GB left · about 12 min"). Each waiting game has two labelled buttons, Download now and Remove; each paused one has Resume (or Try again) and Cancel. The running game has Pause and Cancel, and tapping its name opens its page.

summary: Updates: the version list shows five at a time, so the page opens fast.
changed: Settings > Updates lists versions five at a time, newest first, with Newer and Older buttons.
fixed: The Updates page was slow to fill in and to scroll because it drew every version ever published at once.

summary: A game's page: the badges no longer squeeze into a column on a phone.
fixed: On a phone the badges next to a game's name (Steam, 64-bit, controller, not yet tested) were squeezed by the Play button into a narrow column with the words broken letter by letter. They now wrap onto their own lines and Play sits under them; no badge can break its words any more.

summary: Controller games: a Controller tab on the Steam screen and a controller badge on games.
added: Steam screen: a Controller tab next to All and Installed that lists only games Steam says work with a controller (full or partial support).

A small controller badge on Steam tiles, on your library's tiles, and on a game's pages: green for full controller support, grey for partial. Steam's answer is asked for in batches and kept for a week.

summary: Steam: add installed games back to the library, clearer controls, a shorter game page.
added: Add to library: an installed Steam game that is no longer in the library shows "Add to library" on its tile and its page. It comes back with its Steam link, so it still starts through Steam.
Play on a Steam game's page starts it right there.
changed: The Steam screen: All / Installed is one switch, Select and Refresh are round icon buttons, Downloads shows progress and speed.

A Steam game's page: name, Play or Install, pictures and a short description, then three rows (how it runs on Porthole, Steam reviews, details and files) that open their own pages. Delete files moved to Details and files.

summary: The Steam screen is lighter: one row of controls, quieter tiles.
changed: Search, All / Installed, Select, Downloads and Refresh share one row; the account name and the separate header are gone (the account is in Settings).
Each game's picture shows one badge only when there is something to say (a download, an update, installed). The compatibility pill is on the game's own page.

summary: Settings has six pages instead of fifteen.
changed: Settings: Play (display, power, sound, controls), Steam and JIT, Saves, Updates, App (colour, reports, setup, about) and Advanced (technical options, engine options, log). The groups that used to be separate pages follow one another on the page they now belong to.
Removed the grouping headings and the footnote about technical options in Performance.

summary: A button that opens Shortcuts to make the VPN shortcut.
added: Settings > JIT and tunnel > Your own VPN > Make the shortcut: opens a new shortcut in Shortcuts and fills in the name Porthole VPN.

summary: Your own VPN: Porthole asks before pausing it and helps you turn it back on.
added: When a VPN is on and Porthole needs its own tunnel (to turn on JIT for a game, or to install an update), it asks first, then remembers the VPN was paused.

Afterwards, once the game has closed or the update is done, Porthole runs a Shortcut you choose (Settings > JIT and tunnel > Your own VPN) to turn the VPN back on, or shows a reminder on Home. A VPN with Connect On Demand comes back by itself.

summary: A game's page is short again: Play, three settings, and four doors to the rest.
changed: A game's page shows only Play, Start, Resolution and Power mode, then four rows: Controls and key binds, How it runs for others, More options, About and files. Each opens its own page with a Back button.

summary: A game's page is one page: no tabs, the common settings first, the rest under More options.
added: More options: speed, memory, the engine, launch options and one-time installs sit behind one button instead of five tabs.
changed: A game's page is a single scroll: Play settings (start mode, resolution, power), how it runs for others, controls, key binds, then More options, then About and Files.
Start (through Steam or directly) moved in with resolution and power mode, so no group holds a single setting.

summary: Home no longer scrolls up and down.
changed: The Home page is sized to the screen and stays put; only the row of games moves, sideways.

summary: Home fits a phone held sideways: no scrolling, everything on one screen.
changed: On a phone held sideways, Home drops the small heading, shrinks the attention chips and sizes the game row to what is left, so the name, Play and the whole row of games are visible at once.
fixed: On a phone held sideways the row of games was partly below the screen.

summary: A new look, part 1: dark only, a slim top bar on every device, and a Big-Picture-style Home.
added: Home shows the chosen game's artwork across the back with its name and Play in front, and one row of games along the bottom. Moving along the row changes the chosen game.
changed: One slim bar along the top on iPhone and iPad (section names as plain words, scrolling sideways if they do not fit). The bottom tab bar on iPhone is gone.
The app is dark only; Settings > Theme now has just the accent colour and glow.

summary: Rockstar's launcher: Chromium no longer takes a second copy of itself in the code pool.
changed: A launch that starts a launcher with its own service keeps plain 64-bit programs out of the code pool (they were copied there although nothing runs from the copy). It was an Engine option before, off by default; a game's own setting still wins.
fixed: Rockstar's launcher and its Social Club helper (each a 250 MB Chromium) could not both fit into the code pool.

summary: Rockstar's Social Club installer can run: Windows' shell classes are registered.
changed: A launch that starts a launcher with its own service registers Windows' shell, picture, URL, signature and certificate components once at the start (what a normal Windows setup does when it is made).
fixed: Social Club's setup quit immediately with 'success' and installed nothing, because the taskbar component it asks for had never been registered, so the launcher kept reporting an incomplete installation.

summary: Rockstar launcher: the signature-checking setup now has the program it needs.
added: Windows' registration tool (regsvr32.exe) is part of the app's Windows files, so the launcher's signature-checking component can be registered at the start of a launch.
fixed: The registration step added in 0.50.175 did nothing because the tool it runs was missing.

summary: Game page: a button to run a game's one-time installs again.
added: Under One-time installs on a Steam game's page: Run them all again. It makes the next start run every install (Rockstar's launcher, Social Club, DirectX, Visual C++) again, for when you deleted what they installed or an install stopped half way.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: Windows' signature checking is set up before Rockstar's launcher runs.
changed: A launch that starts a launcher with its own service now also registers Windows' signature-checking component (wintrust.dll) in the game's Windows setup first.
fixed: Rockstar's launcher said the Rockstar Games SDK had an incomplete installation (code 1002); its check of its own library's digital signature could not run because that component had never been registered.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: the launcher waits for memory that is about to be free.
fixed: When the second launcher process started right after the first one ended, the memory of the first was still being held back and the Social Club library could not load; it now waits for it (up to 30 seconds), and the hold-back is 10 seconds instead of a minute.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: Windows' own libraries now really take less memory.
fixed: The saving for the picture and text resources of Windows libraries (0.50.171) did not apply to any of them because of a header size check; it does now.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: freed memory pieces are joined, so the Social Club library finds room.
fixed: The launcher's Social Club library (6 MB) could not be loaded because free memory lay in many small pieces; neighbouring pieces are joined now.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: libraries take much less of the code pool.
changed: In a Steam launch the engine no longer copies the picture and text resources of Windows' libraries into its code pool (shell32 alone was 8.7 MB of 9.5 per program).

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: the recovered memory is no longer handed out too soon.
fixed: A part of a finished program could be given to the next one while one of its stray threads still ran code from it, which ended the app. Recovered memory now waits a minute before it is reused.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: the code pool gets a good part of its lost memory back.
fixed: When a program exits, the memory its libraries used could only be reused as a whole, and a few unusable pages in each block made the engine throw the whole block away (464 MB in one log). The good parts of each block are kept now.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: the launcher no longer freezes on 'Connecting to Rockstar services'.
fixed: The shortened memory copy of the Social Club installer (0.50.166/167) applied its relocation table from the wrong place, which could freeze the whole launcher; it now reads it from the right place.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: the installer's size cut now applies.
fixed: The cut of a huge installer's memory copy (0.50.166) did not apply to the Social Club installer because a small section follows its resources; it does now, and the log lists the sections of big programs.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: huge installers take far less of the code pool.
fixed: Rockstar's launcher restarts itself, and the second copy could not start because memory for libraries ran out; a program with a very large resource section (the Social Club installer) now only has its code part copied.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: the launcher's installers no longer fill the code pool.
fixed: A program that loads an image, finds its place taken and loads it again (Rockstar's Social Club installer, 125 MB) kept every attempt in memory until it quit; the first attempt is now given back.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: Rockstar's launcher can draw its window, and has more room.
changed: A game that starts a launcher with its own background service gets a 1152 MB code pool instead of 896 MB (unless the game has its own pool setting).
fixed: Rockstar's launcher paints its window through Direct2D's GDI interop, which the graphics layer cannot do; it now reads the picture back and draws it itself instead of crashing.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: Rockstar's background service no longer crashes at start.
fixed: With the Steam client and several helper programs running, a newly started program was told about so many libraries of the others that it ran out of room for its own. Rockstar's service crashed on that every time, and the launcher kept restarting it until the app ran out of memory. A program's own libraries now come first.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: the Rockstar launcher no longer stops on an unfinished Direct3D call.
fixed: Rockstar's launcher asks Direct3D 11 to switch its device state once at start-up; that call used to end the launcher on the spot. It is accepted now.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: the Rockstar launcher's Direct2D no longer crashes.
fixed: When a second program started while the first was still loading libraries, the first one's emulator never heard about the libraries it loaded afterwards, so its next call into one of them crashed. Each program now tells its own emulator.

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: Rockstar's launcher no longer stops for a missing Direct2D library.
added: Windows' Direct2D (d2d1.dll), its d3d10_1.dll helper and netprofm.dll are now in the app.
fixed: Rockstar's launcher loaded d2d1.dll late, found none, and ended itself, so RDR2 said 'Unable to launch game, please try reinstalling the game.'

summary: Red Dead Redemption 2: Windows' service manager now runs at every start, not only while Rockstar's installer runs.
fixed: Rockstar's launcher runs RockstarService.exe install and start at every start and found no service manager once its installer was done, so it failed three times and then sat idle with no window. A Steam game whose install scripts include the Rockstar Games Launcher now gets the service manager at every start. env.MADEIRA_DOCK_SERVICES = 1 gives it to any Dock game.

summary: Fix for a 64-bit program crashing at start when its own folder holds a copy of Windows' C runtime (Rockstar's launcher service).
fixed: A 64-bit program that ships its own ucrtbase.dll no longer crashes the emulator at start with an illegal instruction. Rockstar's launcher service installer did exactly this, so Red Dead Redemption 2's Rockstar Launcher setup failed at its last step. The copy in the program's folder is now served from the app's own build. Set env.MADEIRA_APP_LOCAL_UCRT = 1 on a game to keep its own copy.

summary: A game page setting to run a Steam game's one-time installers again.
added: Steam games' pages have a One-time installs choice (under Launch): Run at next start or Skip. After an installer has had its turn the choice goes back to Skip, so a failed one (Red Dead Redemption 2's Rockstar launcher, for example) could not be tried again; now you can.

summary: Experimental: games that draw with OpenGL can now run (not tried on a device yet).
added: OpenGL support, ported from a Madeira fork with OpenGL support. Desktop OpenGL runs through Mesa's Zink on MoltenVK, with Apple's OpenGL ES 3.0 as a fallback; 32-bit OpenGL games and LuaJIT (LOVE) games are covered. The app is about 25 MB larger.

Settings > Engine options > OpenGL: choose the OpenGL driver, turn OpenGL off (to see whether it is what breaks a game), and two opt-in switches from the same work: large address reservations and a short audio buffer.
changed: The launch screen and the FPS readout now count OpenGL frames as well as Direct3D ones.

summary: A per-game controller choice that shows the pad as a HID DualSense too, for games like Hollow Knight: Silksong.
added: On a game's page, Engine > Controller now has "DualSense (HID) and Xbox": that game sees the controller as a HID DualSense and as an Xbox pad, without changing the app-wide Controller type setting. Rumble does not work in this mode.

summary: The log now says whether a game is asking for the controller at all.
added: A [pad] line at 10 s, 30 s and then every minute of a game: how many times the game has asked for the controller (XInput or the HID pad), the mode it is in and which players are connected. 0 means the game is not looking at the controller through either path.

summary: A game that never got going no longer leaves its controller stuck as keyboard and mouse; the Steam overlay change is switched off by default.
changed: The Steam overlay setting added in 0.50.152 now defaults to leaving the overlay alone (the hang it was made for turned out to be a wrong executable); Engine options > Steam overlay > Off renames the overlay DLLs. If you ran 0.50.152 once, the DLLs are put back on the next start.
fixed: Automatic controller mode wrote down "this game ignores the controller" 25 seconds into any run where the game had not read it yet, so a run that never got going (a launcher, a wrong program, a long load) left that game starting as keyboard and mouse for good. It now remembers that only after three minutes, and the verdicts already stored are cleared once.

summary: Hollow Knight: Silksong (and any game that links Steam) no longer hangs at start: Steam's overlay is kept out.
added: Engine options > Steam overlay (default off). Before a game starts, the overlay DLLs in the prefix's Steam folder (gameoverlayrenderer64.dll and gameoverlayrenderer.dll) are renamed with .porthole-off, never deleted; choose On to put them back.
fixed: A game that uses Steam's API loaded Steam's overlay, which hooks the game's graphics and then searched for free executable memory next to each hook, one 4 KB page at a time through 8 GB of address space. The engine refuses executable memory outside its own pool, so the search never ended and the game sat on a blank screen with its main thread waiting (Silksong, 2 million refused requests in the log).

summary: Performance mode now runs up to 120 FPS on a 120 Hz screen.
changed: Performance (Settings > Performance, or a game's own power mode) used to lock games to 60 FPS. On a screen that can refresh above 60 Hz (iPad Pro, iPhone Pro) it now lets a game present as fast as the screen refreshes, up to 120, and holds the screen at its maximum rate while the game runs (the Engine option that holds it is no longer needed for this). On a 60 Hz screen it stays at 60. Balanced and Battery saver are still 30 FPS, and the automatic drop to Battery saver when the device gets hot still applies. A game that draws faster than it can simulate (Factorio's 60 updates a second) gains smoothness, not speed.

summary: The full performance readout now shows the swap file, compressed memory and the paging rate.
added: In the full readout (the expanded one): a Swap file line (how much of the swap file is handed out, with a FULL SOON warning from 90%), what is held in swap now and its peak, requests the swap file refused, and how much it covers; and a Memory line with compressed memory (which iOS counts at full size), file-backed memory and the rate data is being paged in. The numbers come from the engine's own log, so they refresh as often as the engine writes them (every few seconds), and nothing shows until the swap file is in use.

summary: Fix: the app crashed in the middle of a game while writing the performance log's timestamps.
changed: The controller pointer arrow no longer has a shadow (it cost the screen an extra drawing pass every frame) and its refresh slows to a few times a second until the stick is first used.
fixed: A game could end with a crash inside the system's date formatter (ICU), which the performance log created once a second; the timestamp is now written by the C library, which does not touch it.

summary: On-screen controls hide while a controller is in use.
added: While a controller is connected and you use it, the on-screen buttons and sticks step aside; touching the game screen brings them back until you use the controller again. The menu, pencil and keyboard buttons stay. Engine options > Controllers > Hide on-screen controls when a controller is used turns it off.

summary: Force a game to use the controller as keyboard and mouse, and remap controller buttons by pressing them.
added: A switch, Controller as keyboard and mouse, on each game's page (Engine > Controller) and at the top of the in-game Binds sheet. On forces keyboard and mouse for that game; off goes back to Automatic. In the game it applies at once.

Change one by pressing it: in Controller buttons, press a button on the controller (or push a stick) and the app tells you which one it was and offers what it should do. The full list of buttons is still there. Controller buttons is now always shown on a game's page and in the in-game Binds sheet, not only after keyboard and mouse is chosen.

summary: Controller pointer arrow: a way to nudge it up, and log lines to find the cause of the small offset.
added: Engine options > Controllers > Pointer arrow: move up (2 to 24 points) for when the arrow sits a little below where the game's pointer really is. Only the arrow moves. While the arrow shows, the log gets a few [pad-pointer] lines with the numbers it was placed from.

summary: The controller's mouse arrow now follows the game's real cursor, so it is accurate.
changed: The arrow shown when a controller moves the mouse no longer counts the stick's movement itself (it drifted up and to the left of where the game's pointer really was). It now follows the cursor position the engine reports and draws the game's own cursor image, hidden while the game hides its cursor (first-person views). In Steam and the games it starts, where the engine draws the pointer itself, the stick now moves it by absolute position.

summary: Controller rumble from games: a different way of driving the motors that the controller accepts.
fixed: Games' rumble was silent even though the test buzzes: the looping buzz whose strength was changed live would not start on a DualSense. Each motor now plays short buzzes at the strength the game asks for, the same kind of buzz the test plays.

summary: The rumble test now tells you what happened at each step.
changed: Engine options > Test controller rumble tries a plain buzz on all motors, the left and the right, then the way a game's rumble is played, and shows what each step did (or the error) under the button and in the log as a [rumble] test line.

summary: A pointer arrow is drawn when a controller moves the mouse.
added: When the controller works as a mouse and keyboard, an arrow now shows where the pointer is, so you can see what you are about to click (a game running directly draws none of its own). It appears the first time you move the pointer with the stick and stays; a new setting under Engine options > Controllers, Pointer for the controller, can hide it after three idle seconds or turn it off. The first move puts the game's pointer in the middle of the screen so the arrow and the game start together; touching the screen moves both.

summary: Controller rumble: the log now says where it stops, so it can be fixed.
added: Lines starting [rumble] in the game's log: whether rumble is on, which controllers are connected and what their haptics support, each of the game's vibration requests (the first 60), and the reason one was not played (no controller in the slot, no haptics, or the motor failed to start).

summary: A keyboard button at the top of the screen, next to the menu and pencil buttons.
added: A keyboard button in the top bar (next to Menu and the pencil) opens the on-screen keyboard in one tap while a game runs, no trip through the menu. The menu's Keyboard entry is still there.

summary: On-screen key buttons no longer have a Tap / Hold setting: tap it and it taps, hold it and it holds.
changed: A key button in your layouts now goes down when you touch it and up when you let go (never shorter than a normal tap), so a quick tap is a tap and holding it holds the key. The Tap / Hold / Latch choice is gone; what is left is a single Latch on/off switch for keys like Shift or Ctrl that should stay down until pressed again. Layouts you already made keep working: their Tap and Hold buttons both behave this way.

summary: On-screen controls: a Look / Mouse button you can place anywhere, and the tray is easy to drag from.
added: A new button for your layouts: Look / Mouse (in the tray, or under Screen in a control's "Does" list). In a layout where dragging the screen looks around, pressing it makes the screen a normal mouse (menus, clicking) and pressing it again goes back to looking; in a layout without Look it does the reverse. The button shows which mode you are in and turns blue in Mouse mode. The layout's own Look on/off setting is not changed by it. (A set that uses this button cannot be shared to the community yet: the server does not know the new button.)
changed: The tray under + Add: hold a tile for a moment, then drag it anywhere on the screen. A quick swipe on the tray just scrolls it, so the tiles no longer fight the scrolling.

summary: Fix: the on-screen W A S D / arrow stick works again when you drag it (it only registered taps since 0.50.136).
fixed: Dragging the on-screen stick (or any custom control) moved nothing in the game: the editor's gesture recognisers were also active while playing and cancelled the stick's touch as soon as a drag began. They are now on only while the editor is open.

summary: On-screen controls: a new editor. A pencil button is always on screen; drag buttons in, move, resize and change them right on the game.
added: A pencil button next to the menu button while a game runs opens the controls editor over the game itself - no separate menu. It works on the built-in layouts too: the first time you press it, the layout you are using becomes your own editable layout for that game.
Press + Add (or drag from the tray) to put a stick, mouse button, wheel or any key on the screen; tap a tile to drop it at a free spot, or drag it exactly where you want it. "More..." has every key.

Drag a control to move it (it snaps to the screen centre and to other controls, with guide lines); drag the yellow dot on its corner or pinch to resize it; tap one to change what it does, tap/hold/latch, label, size, copy or delete it - all in a panel that stays out of its way.
Presets (mouse and keys, first person, empty), Undo and Redo, and Look on/off sit in the top bar.
changed: The old layout editor bar and its confirmation alert are gone; the menu entry is now "Edit on-screen controls".
fixed: Save-backup file names no longer use DateFormatter (it crashed once right after a game's processes were torn down).

summary: Memory: a swap cut-off that drops by itself when the app's memory gets tight (opt-in), for fast loading without running out of memory.
added: A new setting for a game's own lines: env.MADEIRA_SWAP_AUTO_AT_MB = <MB>. With Swap covers on Large (8 MB+) the game's hot memory stays in RAM, which loads Sons of the Forest about twice as fast, but it uses ~2 GB more and the app is ended by iOS near the end of the load. With this setting, once the app's memory reaches the number you give (for example 4800), everything the game allocates from then on of 1 MB or more goes to the swap file instead. Off unless the line is added.

summary: Fix for the engine update: Steam games started through the Dock (Factorio) were asked for launch option 0 and never started.
fixed: After the engine update, Steam games whose launch options don't start at 0 (Factorio's are 1, 2, 3 and 5) showed 'launch update retry' in the Steam window and never launched: the engine's new Dock configuration always asked Valve's client for option 0. The launch option the app resolves is now passed to it.

summary: Engine update: Madeira's newest 66 changes (MetalFX upscaling, display choices, NVIDIA GPU report, Wine Mono, Steam offline start) merged with all of ours.
added: The engine is now Madeira 48f9764 (66 changes since the last one): MetalFX upscaling per game, device-shaped resolution choices, a per-game NVIDIA GPU report, Wine Mono for .NET Framework programs, Steam's offline start through the Dock, and more fixes for self-modifying code. The settings for the new switches can be typed as lines on a game's Engine page; screens for them come later.
changed: Controller rumble now follows the engine's own rumble path (the app still plays it on the controller's haptics, and Off still tells games the pad has no motors).
Because the engine changed, the compatibility badges start from zero again.

summary: Engine options: a dxmt line now really reaches the graphics layer, and graphics buffers can be kept in the swap file (experimental).
added: Settings > Engine options > Graphics buffers in the swap file (experimental, off by default; the line is buffer-swap-kb in madeira.cfg or a game's own lines). A game's meshes and other buffers are normally counted in full against the app's memory limit; with this on, buffers of at least the chosen size use memory backed by a file instead. Rust's load holds about 2 GB of them when the app is ended. Needs a swap size too (swap-mb). Whether iOS stops counting them is not known until it has been tried on a device: the log's [bufswap] lines show it.
fixed: A dxmt = ... line (madeira.cfg or a game's own lines) was read and logged but never passed to the graphics layer, so options like d3d11.mipClampBC and d3d11.preferredMaxFrameRate did nothing. They are now exported as DXMT_CONFIG at launch (the log shows an [engine] DXMT config line).

summary: Memory: an automatic mode for the swap file that only kicks in when the app's memory gets tight.
added: Settings > Engine options > Swap also keeps the emulator's memory now has Automatic: the game runs at full speed until the app's memory reaches about 3 GB, and from then on what the emulator allocates goes to the swap file. Before, it was all or nothing (always in the file, which slows the game, or never, which left no protection when a server world loaded).

summary: Rust: its Discord plugin can load now, so the memory no longer climbs by gigabytes in a minute.
fixed: Rust's Discord plugin needs qwave.dll, which was missing. The game retried the load hundreds of times and each failed try kept memory, so a few minutes into the menu the app was ended by iOS at about 6 GB. qwave.dll is now in the app.

summary: Steam games: the emulator no longer runs out of its own address range after a few minutes.
changed: In a Steam session the games' and Steam's large per-thread reservations now go to the spare address range (unused without a web browser) before the emulator's own range. Rust ended after about 6 minutes with 'the emulator address band is exhausted' while that spare range was nearly empty.

summary: Steam games get 8 GB more address space when their range runs out (Rust could not load Steam's client library).
changed: For games started through Steam, the engine's spare 8 GB address-space reserve (kept for a web browser that a Steam session does not run) is now handed to the game when its address range is full. Rust filled its 16 GB range, so its Steam library could not load Steam's client library and the game stalled at 99 % loading. Madeira's own app already did this; Porthole did not.
The 0.50.127 early-load attempt is removed (it could not work: Wine ignores the setting it relied on).

summary: Rust: Steam's client library is loaded into the game at its start, before the game's address range fills up.
changed: Rust stalled at 99 % loading because its Steam library could not load Steam's client library late in the run (no free address space). The Dock host now loads it when the game starts. Nothing in the game or in Steam's files is changed.

summary: Rust: starts RustClient.exe with Steam's client running next to it.
changed: Rust's Play button now signs in to Steam as usual and then starts RustClient.exe next to Steam's client (instead of RustClient.exe without Steam, which stalled at 99 % loading, or Rust.exe, which starts Easy Anti-Cheat). The program has to be inside Rust's own install folder.

summary: Rust: Play on the library entry now starts RustClient.exe with Rust's own Steam identity.
added: A known-game fix for Rust (Steam app 252490): Play starts RustClient.exe directly instead of Rust.exe (Easy Anti-Cheat's launcher), and publishes Rust's own Steam app id and folder. Before, a program started this way told the game's Steam library it was another game, and Rust stopped at 99 % loading.

summary: Rust: the missing system library is now really in the app.
fixed: 0.50.123 was meant to add wintypes.dll (Rust's main library needs it) but the app was built without it. It is included now.

summary: Rust: the game's main library can load now (a missing Windows system library was added).
fixed: Games whose main library imports the Windows Runtime buffer interface (Rust shows "Failed to load il2cpp") failed to start because wintypes.dll was not in the app's system libraries. It is now.

summary: A program started without Steam now gets its own log file again.
fixed: Games and programs started with Run directly (or added by path) never made their own file in Documents/logs, only the shared madeira-log.txt. They now write Documents/logs/<program>-<date>_<time>.txt like Steam games do.

summary: Memory: an experimental switch lets the swap file also keep the emulator's own memory.
added: Settings > Engine options > Swap also keeps the emulator's memory (off by default, needs Swap covers set to Wide). Heavy games such as Sons of the Forest are ended by iOS at the memory limit with about 2 GB of the emulator's own memory counted against them; with this on that part can go to storage. Nothing changes unless you turn it on.

summary: Memory: the app now listens for iOS memory warnings and logs how close each game came to running out.
added: While a game runs, iOS memory warnings (warning, critical) are logged as [mem-pressure] lines with the app, free and GPU memory at that moment, and the host's unused malloc memory is handed back to the system (this does not touch the game's own memory).

A [mem-pressure] red zone line when free memory drops under 400 MB and when it recovers, and a [mem-summary] line when the game ends: peak app and GPU memory, least free memory, seconds spent under 1 GB and 500 MB free.

summary: Black Ops 3: the timeline also records the names the game's lookups compare.
changed: The Black Ops 3 timeline (Documents/bo3-timeline) now samples every 20 ms and writes strings.txt: the text its registers point at, to see which function name the game cannot find.

summary: Black Ops 3: the timeline's deep stack snapshot now actually triggers.
fixed: The Black Ops 3 timeline (Documents/bo3-timeline) did not save the deep stack snapshot in 0.50.117 because an early sample from a background thread disabled the test. It saves it now.

summary: Black Ops 3: the timeline keeps the whole call chain when the game enters its endless loop.
changed: The Black Ops 3 timeline (Documents/bo3-timeline) now saves 13 KB of stack when the game's busiest thread jumps far deeper, so the call chain into the endless loop is visible.

summary: Black Ops 3: a timeline of how the game's copy protection enters its endless loop.
changed: While Black Ops 3 starts, the app now saves a short timeline (Documents/bo3-timeline) of its busiest thread: where its stack was and what was on it. The saved game memory (bo3-dump3) is only written for Black Ops 3 now; other games no longer trigger it.

summary: Black Ops 3: the saved game memory now includes the live registers and a short run of samples.
changed: The memory saved for analysis is now written to Documents/bo3-dump3 and includes the live registers, the flags and 96 quick samples of the spinning thread (series.txt).

summary: Black Ops 3: the saved game memory now includes all of its code.
changed: The memory saved for analysis (Documents/bo3-dump2) now includes the game's second code section.

summary: Black Ops 3: when its copy protection spins, the app saves the game's memory for analysis.
changed: When a game spins at full CPU in one place, the app now writes the game's code and stack (about 100 MB) to Documents/bo3-dump so it can be analysed on a computer. Delete the folder afterwards.

summary: Black Ops 3: the log follows more of the code its busy loop calls.
changed: The log now records more of the code a game's busy loop runs and calls. Nothing else changes.

summary: Black Ops 3: its program name now reaches it with the capitals it has on disk.
changed: The engine version changes (bbbf8d0-r20): badges start from the earlier-version results again until games are reported on it.
fixed: Steam's client started Black Ops 3 with its program name in lower case (blackops3.exe). The game now sees BlackOps3.exe, the spelling on disk, which its copy protection may compare.

summary: Black Ops 3: another try at the endless loop in its copy protection (forwarded function names).
changed: The engine version changes (bbbf8d0-r19): badges start from the earlier-version results again until games are reported on it.
fixed: kernel32's forwarded functions now name their target library in capitals (KERNELBASE) like Windows does, which a program that follows such names by hand may need.

summary: Black Ops 3: the system library functions its copy protection looks for now exist.
changed: The engine version changes (bbbf8d0-r18): badges start from the earlier-version results again until games are reported on it.
fixed: Black Ops 3's copy protection looks a function up by name in kernel32 and loops forever when it is missing. kernel32 now also exports the 326 functions Windows 10 has that it lacked; they report "not implemented" if called, and the log names the one the game calls.

summary: Black Ops 3: its copy protection now reads a trimmed copy of ntdll from disk.
changed: The engine version changes (bbbf8d0-r17): badges start from the earlier-version results again until games are reported on it.
fixed: When a 64-bit program reads ntdll.dll from the System32 folder as a file, it now gets a copy of the x64-compatible build cut to the end of its last section instead of the ARM64 build (which had no x64 system-call stubs) or the padded loader copy. This is for Black Ops 3's copy protection.

summary: Black Ops 3: the log compares the three views of the memory its breakpoint is in.
changed: The log now compares the different views of the memory around a game's breakpoint instruction. Nothing else changes.

summary: Black Ops 3: the log shows the code around its breakpoint instruction.
changed: The log now records the code around a game's breakpoint instruction and its stack at that moment. Nothing else changes.

summary: Black Ops 3: the log records the code of its unhandled-exception filter.
changed: The log now records the code of the game's own exception filter and the exception it is asked about. Nothing else changes.

summary: Black Ops 3: the log shows its unhandled-exception filter.
changed: The log now records whether a game sets an unhandled-exception filter and what it answers. Nothing else changes.

summary: Black Ops 3: the log records the filter code behind its breakpoint handler.
changed: The log now records the filter code of a game's exception handler and what its unhandled-exception filter does. Nothing else changes.

summary: Black Ops 3: the log records the code of its breakpoint handlers.
changed: The log now records the code of a game's exception handler that answers a breakpoint. Nothing else changes.

summary: Black Ops 3: the log shows how its breakpoint handlers answer.
changed: The log now records which exception handlers a game registers and what they answer to a breakpoint. Nothing else changes.

summary: Black Ops 3: system files its copy protection loads from disk now work when it runs code in them.
changed: The engine version changes (bbbf8d0-r16): badges start from the earlier-version results again until games are reported on it.
fixed: A program that maps an ARM64EC system file itself and runs code in it called through a connection table the loader had not filled in, which stopped Black Ops 3's copy protection about 25 seconds in. The table is filled in now.

summary: Black Ops 3: an experiment with how it reads ntdll from disk.
changed: One system file (ntdll) is again read from the System32 folder as before, for Black Ops 3's copy protection. Other programs are not affected in a way that matters.

summary: Black Ops 3: the log records the code of its busy loop (wider search).
changed: The log now records the code blocks of a game thread's busy loop, searching further for them. Nothing else changes.

summary: Black Ops 3: the log records the code of its busy loop.
changed: The log now records the code blocks of a game thread's busy loop. Nothing else changes.

summary: Black Ops 3: the log shows more of what its busy thread is doing.
changed: The log now records more of a busy game thread's state. Nothing else changes.

summary: A switch to use LocalDevVPN instead of the app's own tunnel.
added: Settings > JIT and tunnel > Tunnel > "Use LocalDevVPN instead": when on, the app does not start its own tunnel (which replaces any other VPN and sometimes fails to come up); LocalDevVPN has to be on before Play.

summary: Remote testing: a link can show the Steam window instead of the launch screen.
added: porthole://play?exe=...&peek=1, sent from a paired Mac, starts a game and shows the Steam window (the desktop) in place of the launch screen, so a screenshot shows what the game's host prints.

summary: Remote testing from a paired Mac is back (launch a game, install the newest update, read the log).
added: A paired Mac can start Porthole with a porthole:// link as the launch argument -portholeURL to start a library game, stop it, change one game setting line, or install the newest update. Links from anywhere else still need Settings > Advanced > Allow remote-control links, which is off by default.

summary: Black Ops 3: the log now shows what a busy thread is working on.
changed: When one thread of a game runs a long loop, the log now records its registers and the memory it is walking. Nothing else changes.

summary: Black Ops 3: 64-bit programs now get the x64-compatible system files when they read them from disk (the redirect added in 0.50.89 had a typo).
changed: The engine version changes (bbbf8d0-r14): badges start from the earlier-version results again until games are reported on it.
fixed: The System32 redirect for 64-bit programs added in 0.50.89 never matched (an upper-case drive letter in its path test). It does now, so Black Ops 3's copy protection reads the same system files that are loaded.

summary: Black Ops 3: more detail in the log about the system files it opens.
changed: The log now lists the system files a 64-bit program opens, so the cause of Black Ops 3's last stop can be found. Nothing else changes.

summary: Black Ops 3: the system files its copy protection reads from disk are now the right (x64-compatible) ones.
changed: The engine version changes (bbbf8d0-r13): badges start from the earlier-version results again until games are reported on it.
fixed: A 64-bit Windows program that opens a system DLL from the System32 folder now gets the x64-compatible build of it, as it would on Windows for ARM. Black Ops 3's copy protection reads system files from disk, was handed the ARM64 builds and stopped with an access violation about 25 seconds in.

summary: Black Ops 3: its copy protection can now run code from the system files it loads from disk.
changed: The engine version changes (bbbf8d0-r12): badges start from the earlier-version results again until games are reported on it.
fixed: Black Ops 3's copy protection loads clean copies of Windows system files from disk and runs code in them. The engine never told the processor emulator that those copies were executable, so the game was stopped with an access violation after about 25 seconds. The engine now registers such files.

summary: Black Ops 3: a crash while the game reads a system file from disk is fixed.
changed: The engine version changes (bbbf8d0-r11): badges start from the earlier-version results again until games are reported on it.
fixed: Black Ops 3's copy protection maps a Windows system file from disk to compare it with the loaded copy. The engine took that file view for a loaded program and copied more bytes than the view holds, which crashed the game. A file view that is shorter than the program header claims is now left as plain readable memory.

summary: Black Ops 3: a hang inside the engine is fixed (it waited forever while mapping a file).
changed: The engine version changes (bbbf8d0-r10): badges start from the earlier-version results again until games are reported on it.
fixed: Black Ops 3 stopped after its protection phase and never opened a window: the engine's fault handler waited for a lock held by the very thread that had faulted. A thread that faults while holding that lock is now serviced without waiting.

summary: Black Ops 3: the log now says which file it maps and how long it takes.
changed: For large files a program maps into memory, the log now records the file and how long mapping took. Nothing else changes.

summary: Black Ops 3: the program's module list now has Windows' order (the likely cause of its crash).
changed: The engine version changes (bbbf8d0-r9): badges start from the earlier-version results again until games are reported on it.
fixed: Black Ops 3 crashed about 22 seconds in. Its copy protection takes the first module in the program's initialization list to be ntdll and looks a function up in it; on this engine that list started with kernelbase, so the lookup failed and the program called a null pointer. The lists now start the way Windows' do (ntdll first; kernel32 and kernelbase right after it).

summary: Black Ops 3: the crash log now lists the program's module order.
changed: When Black Ops 3 crashes, the log now also lists the order of the modules the program sees. Nothing else changes.

summary: Black Ops 3: the crash log now also shows what its stack points at.
changed: When Black Ops 3 crashes, the log now also lists what the program's stack pointers point at. Nothing else changes.

summary: Black Ops 3: the log now includes its stack at the crash.
changed: When Black Ops 3 crashes, the log now also includes the program's stack around the crash. Nothing else changes.
