summary: Black Ops 3: a wider code dump at its crash.
changed: When Black Ops 3 crashes, the log now includes about 20 KB of the game's code around the crash. Nothing else changes.

summary: Black Ops 3: the call list now also reports how it picked the game's process.
changed: The log line that starts the Black Ops 3 call list now says which program it found, because the list did not appear in 0.50.78. Nothing else changes.

summary: Black Ops 3: the log now lists the Windows calls the game makes.
changed: For Black Ops 3 only, the log now lists each Windows call the game's own code makes (call number, arguments), so the cause of its crash can be found. Nothing else about how games run changes.

summary: Black Ops 3: more detail in the log about where it crashes.
changed: When a game crashes by calling a null pointer, the log now includes the bytes of the code that made the call, so the cause can be worked out. Nothing about how games run changes.

summary: Counter-Strike 2: the crash that ended every run is fixed at its source (a stubbed Windows call).
changed: The engine version changes (bbbf8d0-r8): badges start from the earlier-version results again until games are reported on it.
fixed: Counter-Strike 2 crashed every run, between 95 and 215 seconds in. Its ray-tracing library asks Windows to prefer a processor for each worker thread (SetThreadIdealProcessorEx); Wine's version of that call was an unimplemented stub that reported failure, the library tried to print a warning about it, and printing crashed. The call now reports success (nothing can be scheduled on a chosen processor on iOS anyway).

summary: Counter-Strike 2: thread-pinning requests are accepted whatever the reason they were refused, and the log says which step failed.
changed: A request to pin a thread to a core is now accepted even when the internal server refuses it (nothing is pinned on iOS either way), and the log records the first requests and any failure.

summary: Counter-Strike 2's crash after about a minute and a half is fixed (thread pinning request refused).
fixed: Counter-Strike 2 crashed about 100 seconds in, every time: its ray-tracing library asks to pin its worker threads to core numbers this device does not have, the request was refused, the library tried to print a warning about it, and printing crashed. Such requests are now accepted quietly (nothing is pinned on iOS either way).

summary: More detail in the log when a 64-bit game crashes (Counter-Strike 2 crashes in an audio helper library).
changed: When a 64-bit program faults, the log now records the program's registers and the text its pointer registers point at. Nothing else changes.

summary: Launch options now work for games started through Steam.
fixed: The Launch options row on a game's page was ignored for games from your Steam library (it only applied to programs Porthole runs directly). It is now written into Steam's own settings for that game before each start, so options such as -insecure or -nosound reach the game. Clearing the row removes them.

summary: Room for Ubisoft's own service to start, which its client needs before it can launch Far Cry 6.
changed: Of Ubisoft Connect's helper programs, only the two one-shot ones (an update check and a taskbar-identity helper, which stayed running and used a full core each) are refused; its main service is started. 32-bit programs may now take a ninth address slot while at least 6 GB of address space stays free (it was 8).

summary: Two more 32-bit address slots, so Ubisoft Connect can run its helpers and its service at once.
changed: Ubisoft Connect's UplayService helper programs are started again (the client waits for them: it stayed at "Preparing to launch your game" without them). The engine version changes (bbbf8d0-r6): badges start from the earlier-version results again until games are reported on it.
fixed: 32-bit programs can now use nine address slots instead of seven: two slots were refused only because of a guard page that does not matter. Ubisoft Connect needs about nine programs running at once.

summary: Ubisoft Connect no longer tries to install Steam after the login (Far Cry 6).
fixed: After you logged into Ubisoft Connect it downloaded and ran Steam's installer and stopped going on, because the prefix said Steam lived in another game's folder (a game run outside Steam in the same prefix had overwritten Steam's location). Every Steam-library start now puts Steam's location back to the one Porthole uses.

summary: Frees two address slots so Ubisoft Connect's page-drawing helper can start (the white box).
changed: Ubisoft Connect's two UplayService helper programs (an updater and a taskbar-identity helper) are no longer started. Each one held one of the few 32-bit address slots for ever, so the helper that draws the client's page could not start and the window stayed blank.

summary: Ubisoft Connect's helper processes are allowed to start again (refusing them made Chromium stop with 'GPU process isn't usable').
changed: The Ubisoft Connect client's helper processes are no longer refused or given extra switches by default; their command lines are written to the log in full instead.

summary: Ubisoft Connect's client now runs as one process, and 32-bit helper programs stop copying their files into the code pool.
changed: Ubisoft Connect's client (upc.exe, started for Far Cry 6) now runs in Chromium's single-process mode with software rendering, as Steam's web helper already does, and its helper processes are not started. Before, each helper took one of the few address slots and a code buffer, and the client window stayed blank. The engine version changes (bbbf8d0-r5): badges start from the earlier-version results again until games are reported on it.
fixed: A 32-bit program started by another 32-bit program had every one of its files copied into the code pool, about 230 MB for Ubisoft Connect, and a 196 MB one failed with the pool full. They are no longer copied.

summary: An option to keep big x64 program files out of the code pool, so Far Cry 6 leaves room for Ubisoft Connect.
added: Settings > Engine > Memory > Big x64 programs in the code pool: Keep out of the pool stops the engine copying every x64 program file a game loads into the JIT code pool. Far Cry 6's main file alone took 510 MB of a 1.1 GB pool, which left no room for Ubisoft Connect's helper programs. Off by default (experimental); applies from the next start.
fixed: A 32-bit program that writes into its own read-only code (an inline hook on a page it has not made writable) now works as it does on Windows: the page is made writable for the write and put back. Before, that write failed with an access violation.

summary: A Windows helper process that cannot start because the code pool is full no longer takes the whole app down with it.
fixed: When the code pool was full, starting another 32-bit Windows process (Ubisoft Connect starts several for Far Cry 6) could make the process fault endlessly until the app shut itself down. Only that process now stops, and the app and the game keep running.

summary: Programs that patch their own process's system functions can now write the patch (Ubisoft Connect's client for Far Cry 6).
changed: The engine version changes (bbbf8d0-r4): badges start from the earlier-version results again until games are reported on it.
fixed: A 32-bit program writing into its own memory with WriteProcessMemory (inline hooks over system functions, which launchers and copy protection use) was refused with Access denied. The write now goes straight to memory when the program targets itself, and the emulator is told the code changed. Ubisoft Connect's client stopped at "Error at hooking API" because of this.

summary: More detail in the log about what a 32-bit program does to the system libraries (for the Ubisoft Connect hook error).
changed: The log now records a 32-bit program's memory protection changes, writes and queries on the system libraries' address range. Nothing else changes.

summary: Two experiments for the Ubisoft Connect client behind Far Cry 6, which stops with "Error at hooking API LdrFindResource_U".
added: Settings > Engine > Memory > 32-bit system libraries: keeps the 32-bit Windows system libraries below 2 GB, as on Windows, instead of in the top half of the program's address space. Off by default; applies to 32-bit programs from the next start.
changed: The 32-bit ntdll, kernel32 and kernelbase now begin their functions with the same two-byte no-op Windows uses (mov edi,edi) instead of the equivalent xchg ax,ax, because programs that patch system functions often look for it. The engine version changes (bbbf8d0-r3): badges start from the earlier-version results again until games are reported on it.

summary: The log now shows the text a 32-bit program gives when it reports a fatal error (for the Ubisoft Connect exit behind Far Cry 6).
changed: When a 32-bit program raises a system error report (a hard error) before ending itself, the log now includes its message and caption. Nothing else changes.

summary: More detail in the log when a 32-bit program traps (for the Ubisoft Connect crash behind Far Cry 6).
changed: When a 32-bit program executes a breakpoint or trap instruction, the log now also records the program bytes around it and the top of its stack. Nothing else changes.

summary: Ubisoft Connect is found again after it has been installed for a Steam game (Far Cry 6).
fixed: Far Cry 6 said "Unable to detect Ubisoft Connect installation" even though Ubisoft Connect was installed (its files and desktop icon were there). Its installer's registry entries had been lost, and the game finds it through the registry. At each Steam-library start Porthole now puts back the missing Ubisoft Connect install entry when its files are on disk. Anything already in the registry is left as it is.

summary: Far Cry 6 gets past its first launch step: the Visual C++ runtime pieces it needs are now found.
changed: The engine version changes (bbbf8d0-r2): badges start from the earlier-version results again until games are reported on it.
fixed: Games started from the Steam library (Dock) that need vcomp140.dll (OpenMP), vcamp140.dll, vccorlib140.dll or vcruntime140_threads.dll no longer stop with a missing-DLL error (Far Cry 6's renderer needs vcomp140). The Visual C++ runtime you download in Settings was only put in place for games started directly; the Steam library starts them differently, so these four files were never reachable. If you have not downloaded the runtime, do it in Settings first.

summary: Fixes games that hang at 100% CPU while their copy protection unpacks (Far Cry 6 after the Steam login).
changed: The engine version changes (bbbf8d0-r1): badges start from the earlier-version results again until games are reported on it.
fixed: Far Cry 6 and other games whose copy protection changes the memory protection of a large program file page by page no longer stall. The engine walked the file's whole relocation table, twice, on every one of those changes (about 90 ms each for a 534 MB file, so hours in total); it now finds the few blocks it needs by index.

summary: Steadier controller navigation in the app, and a controller that works as keyboard and mouse in games that never read it.
added: Game details > Controller now has Automatic (the default). If a connected controller has not been read at all by the game about 25 seconds in, it becomes keyboard and mouse for that game (a note appears over the game), and it becomes an Xbox controller again the moment the game starts reading it. The result is remembered per game. Choose Xbox controller, Keyboard and mouse, or the DirectInput option to turn Automatic off for a game.
changed: Controller navigation in the app is rebuilt. The D-pad chooses the item beyond the current one in that direction (before, Down could jump to a neighbouring tile whose centre was a little lower), remembers the column when moving up and down through wider rows, and repeats with hysteresis on the stick (D-pad and stick no longer cancel each other).
fixed: Focus no longer drops to the top-left item after a screen redraws: if the focused item disappears, focus moves to the nearest remaining one.
A mouse or trackpad resting over a list no longer pulls the focus away from where the D-pad put it while the list scrolls.
A controller that connects before its profile is ready is now picked up for app navigation instead of being ignored.

summary: Fixes confirm pop-ups that did nothing, such as Go back and Install in Updates.
fixed: Choosing Install or Go back for a version in Settings > Updates and confirming did nothing. The pop-up closed before the install started. The same fix applies to every other confirmation that picks something from a list first (removing a Steam game, restoring a saves backup, deleting a report).

summary: A changed game program is identified as what it is now; an old Broad swap line moves into Swap covers.
changed: A game that is not from Steam is identified by a fingerprint of its program. The fingerprint is now worked out again when the program file changes (a game update, a patched copy), so its compatibility badge and shared key binds follow the program on disk instead of staying on the old build.

A Broad swap coverage choice left in the engine settings by the earlier Engine options row now shows up as Broad in Swap covers, and the old line is removed so it can not force Broad behind the setting's back.
fixed: The controller rumble entry point is exported from the app in every build configuration.

summary: Undo and Redo in the touch layout editors, a working Audio buffer, and more swap and video memory choices.
added: Undo and Redo while arranging the on-screen controls, in the key-bind sketch editor and in the in-game editor.
Swap covers has a Broad choice (it replaces the separate Broad swap coverage row in Engine options).
Video memory has 512 MB and 1 GB choices.
changed: Audio buffer now sets the engine's audio queue (MADEIRA_AUDIO_LEAD_MS); before, it set a variable the newer audio no longer read, so it did nothing.
The layout editors read out each control to VoiceOver, with actions to move, resize and remove it.
Shared key binds: a set you published follows its game if the game's id changes. The Hub now keeps daily backups of its databases.

summary: New badges: Worked in vX, Somewhat worked in vX, Didn't work in vX.
added: A game with no report yet on the current engine now shows how it ran on the engine reported before it: Worked in v0.50.34, Somewhat worked in v0.50.34, or Didn't work in v0.50.34, with the app version it was reported on. The engine mostly adds support, so a game that worked then usually still does; a game that did not work then may well work now. The badge is outlined to show it is a past result, not a verdict. It appears on the library tiles, the game's page, the Steam tab and the compatibility list. Once someone reports on the current engine, that verdict takes over.
changed: Past reports no longer turn into Not yet tested when the engine updates; Not yet tested now only means nobody has reported the game at all.

summary: Controller rumble, automatic save backups, and "use what works for others".
added: Controller rumble. When a game asks the controller to vibrate it does, with the left (heavy) and right (light) motors felt differently. Needs a controller with haptics. Settings > Engine options has Controller rumble (Off, Light, Medium, Strong) and a Test button. Works for 64-bit and 32-bit games; not for player 1 set to a HID controller.

Automatic save backups. When a game ends, your saves and settings are zipped into Files > Porthole > Saves backups. The newest five are kept, nothing is written when nothing changed, when the saves are over 150 MB or the phone is nearly out of space. Settings > Saves lists them and restores any of them, and has a Back up now button and a switch.

Use what works for others, at the top of a game's Performance section: the settings that most people who say the game works great use (power mode, swap, video memory and more), set against yours. Apply the ones that differ for this game with one tap, and undo it. Nothing changes until you tap.

summary: Edit and test your controls while the game runs.
added: The in-game menu has Binds and Edit and test on-screen controls. Binds opens over the running game: pick the bind set in use (it applies at once, no restart), make a new set from your current controls, and edit a set's controller binds and layout.

Edit on-screen controls on the game itself: drag a control to move it, tap it to change what it does, its label, how it presses (tap, hold or latch) and its size, add buttons, mouse buttons and sticks, and turn drag-to-look on or off. Switch between Editing and Testing to try the controls without leaving the game. Every change is saved to the bind set as you make it.
With no custom layout yet, the editor makes a new set from a starting layout (mouse and keys, first person or empty) and uses it; your other settings are not changed.
fixed: The sticks in a bind set's touch layout did not respond to touch; they do now.

summary: Share bind sets: browse, rate, add and share key binds and touch layouts for a game.
added: A game's Binds section has a Community group. Browse the controller binds and touch layouts other people shared for that game, sorted by rating, downloads or newest, read their reviews, and add one to your own sets. An added set is a copy you can change and is only used when you pick it.
Rate a shared set with a thumb and an optional comment, and report one that is spam. Comments, and the names, notes and control labels authors type, show to others only after they have been approved.
Share one of your own sets from its page: it is sent without any name or account of yours, can be updated, and can be taken down again at any time.
Sharing needs the update server to be running the new sharing service. Until it is, Browse and Share say so.

summary: Bind sets: several sets of controls per game, one in use at a time.
added: A new Binds section on every game's page. Make several named bind sets for a game and pick the one to use; each can hold controller binds, an on-screen touch layout, or both. Standard keeps the game's own Controls and Engine settings exactly as they were, and a set never changes them.
A touch layout editor: drag keys, mouse buttons, the wheel and sticks around a sketch of the screen, change what each does and how big it is, and choose whether dragging looks around.
Export a set to a .portholebinds file and import one back.

summary: New engine options: controllers in games, per-game AVX and frame generation, save backups, shortcuts and more. Nothing that was already set changes.
added: Controllers now reach games. A paired controller appears to the game as an Xbox pad (up to four players). Settings > Engine options can show player 1 as a DualSense or a generic gamepad instead, and add a DirectInput joystick.
Controller as keyboard and mouse, for games with no controller support: choose it on a game's Engine page, change what each button does, and set the right stick's up and down speed.

A new Engine section on every game's page: AVX and AVX2, frame generation (experimental), CPU cores reported, Direct3D 9 anisotropic filtering, reduced-precision x87, a working folder, and the game's own engine lines.

A new Settings > Engine options page with switches the engine has but Porthole had no screen for: JIT code pool size, memory reported to games, swap floor and broad swap coverage, Eco priority, CPU cores, Direct3D 12 tuning, Direct3D 9 frontend, MP4 video, holding the screen at its top refresh rate, and the controller options. Every row starts on Default and only writes when you change it.
Start games sooner: Wine starts as soon as its server is ready instead of after a fixed 2 second pause (Engine options can turn it off).
In the game's menu: capture the next frame, change the GPU sync mode, and turn Eco mode on or off. The full stats readout now also shows how busy the GPU is and the busiest thread.
Settings > Saves: back up every game's saves and settings to one zip and restore them. A game's Engine page copies a Home Screen shortcut link (porthole://play) for the Shortcuts app.
Programs that are batch files (.bat or .cmd) now run through cmd.exe.

summary: The game engine is updated to the latest Madeira (232 upstream changes).
changed: The game engine (Madeira with Wine, FEX and DXMT) is brought up to date. It includes faster game start, more memory-saving options, native D3D12 improvements, audio pacing, many crash fixes and Steam Cloud saves. Our own fixes (thread-table reuse, SIMD stores, Steam launch option, installer repaint, the day/night fix, the bigger code pool) are kept.
Compatibility badges show "Not yet tested" until games are reported on this engine.

summary: iPhone layout fixes and working (i) pop-ups.
changed: The (i) explanations now open as a small sheet from the bottom instead of an arrow pop-up. It is sized to the text and scrolls when the text is long, on iPhone and iPad.
fixed: The (i) pop-ups were cut off on iPhone and iPad.
iPhone Home: the Continue playing card was too short, so the game name was cut off. It now grows to fit its text.
iPhone Steam tab: the account name, the Downloads and Refresh buttons and the filter buttons wrapped one letter per line. The header stacks on a narrow screen and the filters wrap as whole buttons.
iPad: the Porthole name in the top bar was squeezed to one letter in a narrow window. The top bar now drops the name, then the status chips, before squeezing the tabs.
Buttons keep their label on one line.

summary: The update server settings are gone from the app.
changed: Settings > Updates no longer has an update server section. The server a build talks to is set when the build is made, not in the app.

summary: The update server address is no longer shown in the app.
changed: Settings > Updates no longer shows the update server address or token when the build carries its own server. Builds without one still ask for it. Pressing the Installed version seven times shows or hides the section.

summary: Less to fill in for updates.
changed: The setup guide no longer asks for the update server address and token. Settings > Updates keeps the address, and the token is behind one row (Hub token), since it is only used when the device cannot install an update by itself.

summary: Clearer buttons in setup, and fixes for cut-off pop-ups and the Downloads picture.
changed: Status lines in the setup guide and Settings (like 'Allowed' or 'Pairing file ready') are now plain text with no card, and the one thing to press on a page is filled with the accent colour, so you can tell which is the button.
The pairing screen says 'this device' instead of 'this iPhone'.
fixed: Downloads: the card for the game downloading now kept the first game's picture when the queue moved on; it shows the right game now.
The (i) pop-up with long text (pairing credits) was cut off at the bottom of the screen; long text now scrolls inside a fixed height.
The sides of the options in drop-down lists (like Power mode) were cut off; they have room around them now.

summary: Two fixes from the test checklist.
fixed: Changing a colour, the glow or the appearance no longer jumps Settings back to the Display page; it stays on the page you were on.
Steam tiles now show their compatibility badge (or 'Not yet tested') all the time, not only after you interact with a tile. Opening one game's page no longer wipes the badges of the others.

summary: Tidier game page: one Play button and the art as the whole background.
changed: A game's page now uses its art as the full-screen background, softened and darkened, instead of a banner across the top.
fixed: The game page showed two Play buttons. The first section is now called Launch, with a settings icon, so Play appears only once, at the top right.

summary: Steam cloud saves download several at a time.
changed: Before a game starts through Steam, its cloud files (saves and settings, usually a few MB or less each) are now fetched up to six at a time instead of one after another. Each file is still checked against Steam's checksum, newer local copies are still kept, and nothing is ever uploaded.

summary: Pick several Steam games and download them in one go.
added: Steam > Select turns on checkboxes: press games to pick them (installed and downloading ones are greyed out), then Download N. There are Select all and Clear buttons, a running total of the size against your free space, and it queues as many as fit, in list order, then opens the Downloads page.

summary: A Downloads page for Steam: what is downloading, how fast, and the queue in your order.
added: Steam > Downloads shows the game downloading now (percent, size, speed, time left) and the games waiting. Move a waiting game up or down, start it now, pause it or remove it; Pause all and Resume all are at the top. The button on the Steam tab shows the live speed.
Paused and failed downloads are listed with Resume / Try again and Cancel.

summary: The Steam tab opens faster and keeps its place when you come back from a game's page.
changed: Steam tile pictures are saved on the device after the first time and are only fetched for tiles near the screen, so a long library fills in around where you are.
fixed: Going back from a Steam game's page no longer jumps to the top of the list and reloads every picture; the list stays where you left it.
The Steam list no longer reads each game's install record from disk several times per redraw, which made scrolling and download progress sluggish with a big library.

summary: Every screen now works with a controller, and each Steam game has its own store page.
added: Steam games have their own page, installed or not: trailers and screenshots, the description, Steam's rating and reviews, developer and release date, the version, system requirements, and how it runs on Porthole with a button to read or write reports. The pictures and text come from Steam's public store page.
Steam tiles show a compatibility badge, and pressing one opens its page. X still installs, pauses or resumes without opening it.
Reports, the setup guide, Add a game, the artwork picker and pairing were rebuilt for the D-pad. Explanations moved behind the (i) buttons.
changed: Pressing a Steam game no longer starts a download straight away; the Install button is on its page.
fixed: Reports, the setup guide and the add-a-game screens did nothing when used with a controller.

summary: Launch screen fix for directly started games, matching page backgrounds, and controller navigation in Settings and the game page.
added: Settings was rebuilt: a grouped list of pages on the left, the page on the right. Every row works with the D-pad: A presses, Left / Right changes a choice or a slider, B goes back. Short explanations moved behind the (i) buttons.

A game's page was rebuilt: its art on top with Play, and sections (Play, Performance, Controls, Compatibility, Details) you switch between without leaving the page. Settings that differ from the app-wide ones say Default until you pick your own.
changed: Every page now has the same deep gradient background as the top bar, instead of black or very dark panels.
fixed: The launch screen stayed up for a game started directly (Factorio, for example) even though the game was running. It now goes away when the game puts its first picture on screen.
Choosing a colour scheme works on every page.

summary: A new look: glowing game tiles, a launch screen with the game's art, controller navigation and your own colours.
added: Home: a featured card for the game you played last with Play right on it, then every game as a picture tile. The selected tile glows. Short chips at the top for things that need attention; tap the (i) for details.

A launch screen from the moment you press Play: the game's artwork behind a glowing porthole that fills as it goes, the steps (JIT, Steam, sign-in, loading), the settings it is starting with, and a Cancel button. It stays until the game's own window appears.
Controller and keyboard navigation: D-pad or arrow keys move between tiles, A / Return selects, B / Escape goes back, LB and RB switch sections. X plays the selected game.
Settings > Appearance: six colour schemes, your own colour, glow strength and a moving-background switch.
changed: The tab bar became a top bar with the Porthole mark (a bar at the bottom on a phone held upright). Steam, Reports and Settings keep their old layouts for now and get the new look in the next build.

summary: 2560 × 1440 is gone from the resolution list.
changed: At 2560 × 1440 Factorio's window never became the active one, so it ignored the mouse (no cursor, clicks did nothing). The size is removed; the list now stops at 1920 × 1080. If you had chosen it, the app-wide or game setting quietly goes back to the default 1280 × 720.
fixed: Mouse and cursor not working after choosing 2560 × 1440.

summary: Choose the resolution games run at, for every game or one at a time.
added: Settings > Display > Resolution: the size of the screen games see, from 640 × 360 up to 2560 × 1440, plus "Screen shape" sizes that match your device's screen so the picture fills it without bars. The default stays 1280 × 720.
Each game's page has its own Resolution (Default follows the Settings choice). It applies the next time the game starts, and the log shows the size used.
changed: Games used to always get a 1280 × 720 screen. Games that draw at the desktop's size now draw at the size you choose; games that pick their own resolution can choose any size up to it. Higher sizes need more memory and speed, and the largest is marked heavy.

summary: Engine 40d5e74-r4: a larger code pool for games that don't need the fixed-address window.
added: Settings > Advanced > "Bigger code pool when the game allows it" (on by default). Turn it off to go back to the previous behaviour.
changed: The emulator reserved 128 MB of memory at 0x140000000 for the rare game that can only load at one fixed address (Red Dead Redemption 2), and that reservation cut the code pool from the 896 MB asked for to 544 to 635 MB. Porthole now reads the game's programs before launch and, when none of them needs that spot, gives it back so the pool fits in one piece. Games that need it keep it. This is a new engine (r4): compatibility badges start again from "Not yet tested".

summary: Games that need Steam's shared files (Black Ops 3) now get them installed before they start.
added: Before a Steam launch, Porthole checks whether the game takes depots from "Steamworks Common Redistributables" (Steam app 228980) and, if that app is not installed, downloads it with its own downloader. The starting screen shows the progress.
changed: Black Ops 3 and similar games were refused by Steam with "required app 228980 not ready" and waited forever: Valve's client queues that download but never starts it. If Steam reports that wait anyway, Porthole remembers it and installs the shared files at the next start.

summary: The exit fix from 0.50.15, this time actually in the app.
changed: 0.50.15 was published with the old x86 translator file inside it (the packaging step used a stale copy), so it does not have the exit fix. This build has it: a game started through Steam can finish exiting, so Steam sees it end and can upload its Steam Cloud files. Same engine as 0.50.15 (r3). Skip 0.50.15.

summary: Engine 40d5e74-r3: a game started through Steam can finish exiting, so Steam sees it end.
changed: Factorio started through Steam never finished exiting: after the game closed, the x86 translator touched an object it had already destroyed and crashed, so Steam's client never saw the game end and never uploaded its Steam Cloud files. The translator now skips that work once the object is gone. This is a new engine (r3), so compatibility badges start again from "Not yet tested"; earlier reports stay visible as earlier.

summary: Steam's client now has a language, so Factorio started through Steam can find its text.
changed: Factorio started through Steam showed "Unknown key: …" on every label. Valve's client in the prefix had no language at all (the registry value it reads was never set, and it rewrote the game's install record with empty language entries), so it gave the game none. Porthole now sets Steam's language to English in the prefix before a Steam launch and fills the install record's language entries when they are empty. 0.50.13 only handled records with no language blocks, which Valve's client had already replaced.

summary: Steam installs now record their language, so games started through Steam can find their text.
changed: A game's Steam install record had no language entry, so Steam's "what language is this game in?" had no answer. Factorio started through Steam showed "Unknown key: …" on its menus. Installs now record English, and installs from older builds are repaired just before each Steam launch (a record Steam itself wrote is left alone).

summary: Steam Cloud saves now go to the user folder games actually use.
changed: 0.50.11 downloaded your Steam Cloud saves but put them in the Windows user folder called "mythic" (a name inside the prefix template), while games run as "mobile", so Factorio did not see them. Cloud files now go to the same user folder Wine runs games as, worked out the same way the runtime does. The copies already in "mythic" are not used and can be deleted (users/mythic/AppData/Roaming/Factorio).

summary: Steam Cloud download: read Steam's file names correctly, and say what it decided for each file.
added: The Steam Cloud download now logs the file list Steam sent and what it did with every file (downloaded, already current, skipped and why), so a problem can be read straight from the log.
changed: 0.50.10 reached Steam and got your 11 Factorio cloud files, but skipped all of them. Steam lists file names relative to a short table of folder prefixes, which the first version ignored. Names are now completed from that table before choosing where each file goes, and a file whose platform list is empty is treated as meant for Windows.

summary: Steam Cloud saves are downloaded before a Steam game starts.
added: Before a game starts through Steam, Porthole now downloads your own Steam Cloud files for it (for example Factorio's world saves) when they are missing on this device, then starts the game. Valve's client doesn't do this step when started this way, so games came up with none of your cloud saves. It only reads from Steam: nothing is uploaded, each file is checked against Steam's checksum before it is saved, a newer file on this device is never replaced, and an older one is kept as a .porthole-backup copy. Settings > Steam has a switch for it. Saves made here are not uploaded yet.

summary: Factorio's Steam launch, second try.
changed: 0.50.8 chose the right Steam launch option for games whose list doesn't start at 0, but it read the game's launch list from the library saved by an older build, which didn't record the numbers, so it still asked for option 0. When the saved list doesn't have the numbers, Porthole now fetches that one game's list from Steam just before starting it.

summary: Games that Steam numbers differently now start through Steam.
changed: Starting a game through Steam always asked Valve's client for the game's launch option number 0. Some games (Factorio) don't have a number 0, so Steam answered "entry for launch option 0 not found" and Porthole gave up after two minutes with "Steam did not finish loading this game's configuration". Porthole now looks up the right number from the game's own launch list and tells the Steam helper which one to use. Games that start at 0 behave as before.

summary: Assetto Corsa now starts its real program.
added: Assetto Corsa: Porthole starts acs.exe, the game itself, directly instead of AssettoCorsa.exe. That file is a .NET launcher, which can't run here (Wine reports that Mono is missing and the program exits at once), and Steam's own launch tries to run the same file. Porthole also gives the game its own Steam identity for this start.

summary: Assetto Corsa no longer crashes the moment it starts.
changed: New game engine version (40d5e74-r2): compatibility badges start fresh for it, older reports stay visible as earlier ones.

Assetto Corsa (a 32-bit game) crashed within seconds of starting in direct mode, on a kind of memory write the engine could not carry out (a 128-bit vector store with a 32-bit register offset). The engine now handles that and the related vector store forms.

summary: The game engine no longer runs out of thread slots.
changed: New game engine version (40d5e74-r1): compatibility badges start fresh for it, and older reports stay visible as earlier ones.

The Forest froze when you started a world: the game was creating hundreds of short-lived audio threads, and the engine's table of threads (512 entries) only gets entries back when the whole game ends. Once it was full, new threads were handled as if they belonged to another process. The engine now reuses the entry of a thread that has finished.

summary: The Forest: the next thing that used up the emulator's code memory.
changed: The Forest got further after the last fix, but froze again once the world started loading: its short-lived threads each load and unload a small Windows audio-priority library (avrt.dll), and the emulator never gets that memory back until the game ends. It ran out again after about 290 reloads. Porthole now tells Wine not to load that library for this game.

summary: A fix for The Forest freezing at the main menu.
added: Known-problem fixes for individual games. The first is The Forest: Porthole now sets aside its Oculus VR plugin (OVRPlugin.dll, renamed to OVRPlugin.dll.porthole-disabled in the game's own folder) before it starts. The plugin could never load here, but each failed attempt used up about 28 MB of the emulator's limited code memory until it ran out and the game froze at the main menu.

summary: Compatibility badges load again.
added: The log now says whether the compatibility badges were loaded, or why not.
fixed: Compatibility badges (and the new Not yet tested badge) were never loaded when the app opened, so the Library showed none. They now load when the app opens, when your games change, and whenever you come back to the app.

summary: Compatibility badges follow the game engine, not the app version.
added: A grey "Not yet tested" badge on games nobody has reported on yet, in the Library and on the game's page.
Each report now says which version of the game engine (the Madeira layer) it was made on. Reports from older engines stay in the list, marked as earlier, but no longer count toward the badge.
changed: Updating the app no longer asks you to report on a game again, and no longer resets its badge: only a new game engine does that.
Sending a report again on the same engine replaces your earlier one; on a new engine it adds a new report.

summary: A new name behind the scenes, and the licence notices.
added: Settings > About and credits > Licences now lists the JIT library's licence (MPL-2.0), where its source code is, and the licences of the libraries inside it.
changed: Porthole has a new app identity (site.portholehq.app). iOS treats it as a new app: delete the old copy first, then install this one. Your signing profile must include the new App IDs (the app, .jithelper and .tunnel).
iOS now shows "Pair with Porthole" when you make a pairing file on the device.
From here on, versions are 0.50.x until the first public release.

summary: Stricter network security.
changed: Porthole now requires https for everything on the internet. Addresses on your local network (for example an update server at home) can still use plain http.

summary: In-app updating: asks iOS the way sideloading tools do.
changed: The in-app install now asks iOS to install the way sideloading tools do for a developer-signed app, and if iOS does not answer within 25 seconds it tries the next way. The log shows which one iOS answers.

summary: Updates: pick any version, reinstall or go back.
added: Settings > Updates now lists every version on the update server, with 'Install again' for the one you have and 'Go back to this' for older ones.

summary: Updating the app from inside the app: no more silent hang at 0%.
changed: The in-app install now writes every step to the log, shows 'waiting for iOS to start (n s)' instead of a frozen 0%, and gives up with a clear message after 90 seconds of silence (then uses the update server if one is set up).

If another VPN that reaches the device (for example LocalDevVPN) is already on, the in-app install uses it instead of Porthole's own connection, because Porthole's own connection is part of the app being replaced.

summary: The setup guide now fills the screen on iPhone too.
changed: The setup guide opens full screen on iPhone as well as iPad.

summary: On iPad the setup guide now fills the screen.
changed: On iPad the setup guide opens full screen instead of as a floating sheet. On iPhone it is unchanged.

summary: A clearer, friendlier setup guide.
added: The setup guide remembers where you stopped, shows 'Step 2 of 5' with what is needed, recommended or optional, and the last page lists what is left; tap a line to jump back to it.
changed: The setup guide is rewritten in plain words: it explains JIT, the pairing file and the VPN prompt, merges Steam and your first game into one 'Add your games' step, and says 'Skip for now' on a step you have not finished instead of a silent 'Next'. It is larger-text friendly and centred on iPad.

summary: Steam downloads try every nearby download site and keep the fastest.
changed: Steam downloads now try a server from each nearby site (for example Atlanta, Dallas, Los Angeles) at the start and keep using whichever answers fastest on your connection, instead of only the first few servers on Steam's list.

summary: Steam downloads pick the fastest servers and start faster.
changed: Steam downloads now send each request to whichever of Steam's servers is answering fastest, avoid ones that are slow or failing, start with more files in flight and can use up to 64 at once. The log shows how fast each server is, so a slow download can be diagnosed.

summary: Fixes Steam downloads that stopped with "a chunk did not check out".
changed: The download speed shown now counts everything coming over the network, and the log gets a speed line every 10 seconds.
fixed: Steam downloads no longer fail with "a chunk did not check out" on games that use a certain kind of compressed file (this also made downloads look very slow, because the same files were fetched again and again).

summary: Steam sign-in, your game list and downloads are now Porthole's own.
changed: Steam sign-in, the list of games you own and game downloads have been rewritten as part of Porthole (the Madeira Steam client code is gone). You need to sign in to Steam once more after updating. Games already installed stay installed; a download that was only half done starts again.
Downloads adjust how many files they fetch at once to the speed of your connection.

summary: Microsoft's Visual C++ runtime is now downloaded from Microsoft inside the app.
added: A new setup step, 'Windows components' (also in Settings > Advanced, and as a notice on the Library until it is done): downloads Microsoft's Visual C++ runtime (about 25 MB) straight from Microsoft, checks it is the genuine file, and keeps it on the device.
changed: The app no longer carries Microsoft's runtime files inside it. If you have not downloaded them yet, do it once from the notice on the Library: games that need Microsoft's C++ runtime will not start without it.

summary: New Licences screen, and the project is now free software (GPL-3.0-or-later).
added: Settings > About > Licences and source code: the licence, credits, third-party notices and licence texts, and where the source code is and how to rebuild it. They are inside the app, so they always match the copy you have.

summary: Behind-the-scenes clean-up. Nothing changes in how the app looks or works.
changed: The app no longer has its builder's server address, app names or computer paths built into it. Your games, settings and sign-ins are untouched.

summary: The app is now called Porthole.
changed: The app has a new name: Porthole. The name on the home screen, in the Files app, in your signing app and in the permission prompts has changed. Your games, settings, pairing file and sign-ins are untouched, because the app is still the same app underneath.

summary: If iOS won't start the tunnel after an update, the app now tells you to restart the device.
changed: When iOS refuses to start the tunnel straight after an app update, Play now stops and says to restart the device, instead of failing later with a vague message. A restart clears it; your games and settings are not affected.

summary: When iOS refuses to run the tunnel, the app now says why immediately instead of waiting.
changed: If iOS starts the tunnel and ends it again within moments, the app now fails at once, writes iOS's own reason to the log, and moves on to the next repair step, instead of waiting out a 25 second timeout three times.

summary: The tunnel repairs itself after an update, with a Reset button and a clearer log. No reinstall needed.
added: Settings > JIT and tunnel > Troubleshooting > Reset the tunnel: deletes the app's VPN setting so a fresh one is made. Games and settings are not touched; iOS asks you to allow the VPN again.
When the tunnel can't start, the log now says what iOS reported and how the tunnel extension was signed, and records each status change.
changed: If the tunnel still isn't up after two tries, the app deletes its own VPN setting and makes a new one automatically (what deleting and reinstalling the app used to do).
Turning the tunnel on while it is already being turned on waits for that attempt instead of starting another.
fixed: After an update the tunnel could refuse to connect until the app was deleted and reinstalled.

summary: The on-screen controls now appear when a Steam game's display first shows, without rotating.
fixed: When a game started through Steam, the Menu and controls were hidden behind the game's picture until you rotated the device. They are now brought to the front as soon as the picture appears.

summary: Switch touch controls while playing, and the Steam status text now clears itself.
added: The in-game Menu has a 'Controls' button that switches between mouse-and-keys and first-person touch controls while you play. The choice is remembered for that game.
fixed: Starting a game through Steam left a line of status text at the top of the screen for the whole game. It now stays only while it is useful and goes away a few seconds after the game is running.

summary: A new layout for iPhone and iPad: tabs and a sidebar, a page for every game, cleaner Settings, and a much better way to add games.
added: Library, Steam, Compatibility and Settings are now sections: a tab bar on iPhone and a sidebar on iPad.

Tapping a game opens its own page: big artwork, Play, and everything about the game grouped by what it does (how it starts, performance, controls, compatibility, files). Anything left on Default follows the app-wide setting.
Adding a game starts with three clear choices (import a folder, download from Steam, run an installer) and lists the games already in the app, each with the right program picked for you.

When a game folder has several programs, the app picks the most likely one and offers the rest on request. Uninstallers, crash reporters and redistributable installers are tucked away instead of listed.
The Steam section is a full-width grid of cover art with each game's progress and button, so it uses the whole iPad screen.

Settings is split into pages (Appearance, Performance, Controls, Sound, JIT and tunnel, Steam, Updates, Compatibility reports, Setup, Advanced, Log, About) with a plain explanation under each setting. On iPad the pages sit beside the list.
An About page that credits the projects this app is built on.
changed: A game that starts through Steam now says so next to the Run directly choice, and explains that games which check Steam will freeze if run directly.
The Library shows things that need attention (JIT waiting, setup, an update, a download in progress) as one tidy list of notices above the games.

summary: Compatibility reports now share the game's settings, so people can reproduce a result.
added: A report can include the settings the game ran with: started through Steam or run directly, power mode, swap, video memory, audio cushion, shader math, Wine desktop display and control layout. Launch options you typed are never shared. There is a 'Share my settings for this game' switch on the report form, showing exactly what would be sent.
Each report on a game's page shows the settings it used, and the page has a 'When it works great, people use' section with the most common setting for each.

summary: Report how a game runs without leaving it.
added: The in-game Menu has a 'Report how it runs' button. It opens the compatibility report form over the running game, with the numbers measured so far this session (average and low FPS, how hot the phone got). The game keeps running behind it, and reporting from here means you aren't asked again after the game ends.

summary: Compatibility reports: see how games run on phones like yours, and add your own report.
added: Every game card shows a compatibility badge (Works great, Playable, Doesn't work) built from reports other people sent, taking your own phone model into account when there are reports for it.

A game's page has a Compatibility section: the badge, how it does on each phone, every report, and a button to write one. Reports include what the app measured (average and low FPS, how hot the phone got) automatically.
A searchable Compatibility screen (Library > + menu) lists every game anyone has reported, including games added from Files.
After you play for 5 minutes or more, the Library asks how the game ran. If the app closed on its own while a game was running, it asks whether it crashed.

For games that did not come from Steam you pick where the files came from from a fixed list (no typing). Reports marked 'somewhere else' stay private. Notes are checked by a person before they appear.

Settings > Compatibility reports: turn badges and the prompt off, see and delete your own reports, or start a fresh reporting identity. No account or code is needed; reports are signed with a random key kept on the phone.

summary: Faster Steam downloads: more chunks at once, adjusted automatically, with timing in the log.
added: The Steam downloader writes [steam-perf] lines to the log every 10 seconds (network speed, disk speed, and how long each step takes per chunk, per server) and a summary at the end, so slow downloads can be diagnosed.
changed: Steam downloads now keep 16 chunks in flight instead of 8, and raise or lower that (8 to 48) depending on whether more connections actually make the download faster.

summary: Updates can install directly on this iPhone, with no upload to your Mac.
added: Updating the app no longer has to go through the Hub: once it is signed on the phone, the app copies it to iOS's own installer over the in-app tunnel and installs it (needs the pairing file from setup). Nothing is uploaded anywhere, and no Hub token is needed for this.
changed: If the direct install fails, the app falls back to the Hub upload when a Hub token is saved, and otherwise shows what went wrong.

summary: Setup guide starts on the in-app JIT method on iOS 27.
changed: On iOS 27 or later a first-time setup preselects 'In the app (pairing file)', so the 'Get one on this iPhone (no computer)' button is the first thing on the JIT page.

summary: Pairing on the iPhone: fixes for 'The connection was interrupted'.
added: The pairing screen has a 'Details (for troubleshooting)' section with a step-by-step trace (also written to the log as [pairing] lines), and tells you when a try failed so you can tap 'Pair with ...' again.
fixed: Pairing from Settings failed with 'The connection was interrupted': the app stopped advertising itself the moment the iPhone connected, which the iPhone treats as the host vanishing. It now keeps advertising until pairing finishes, and keeps listening if a connection drops or a wrong code is typed.
The pairing maths no longer makes the iPhone wait: the code and keys for each try are prepared in advance and the app is compiled with optimisation (it ran about 15 times slower unoptimised).

summary: Get a pairing file on the iPhone itself (iOS 27).
added: On iOS 27 or later you can make the pairing file without a computer: Setup guide > JIT > 'Get one on this iPhone', or Settings > Connection > 'Get a pairing file on this iPhone'. Tap Start, open Settings > Privacy & Security > Developer Mode > 'Pair with Porthole', and type the six-digit code the app shows. The pairing file is saved and In-app JIT is selected. The app stays alive while you are in Settings (silent audio and a background task), shows the code in a notification, and credits the idevice and StikPair projects.
The app asks for Local Network permission the first time, and advertises itself on the network only while you are pairing.

summary: The first Play after installing or updating starts the tunnel.
fixed: The very first start of the tunnel after the app was installed or updated gave up after 4 seconds, before iOS had finished starting it, so Play failed. It now waits up to 25 seconds, asks iOS to start it again if it is still off after 6, retries up to three times, and re-saves the VPN setting if iOS reports it stale, disabled or invalid. The log shows each attempt.

summary: Settings fixes.
fixed: Tapping Log (or Setup guide, or Updates) in Settings no longer opens the other two as well: closing one sheet used to open the next. The same fix applies to the Steam screen's Refresh / Sign out buttons and the Updates screen's buttons.
'JIT method' was shown twice in Settings; the other menu rows (swap coverage, video memory) are tidied the same way.

summary: A calmer, more native design.
changed: Redesigned to look like a polished iOS app rather than a themed one: neutral system-style surfaces (true black in dark mode, soft grey in light), the standard iOS type, one flat accent colour, no gradients, glows, shadows or heavy borders.

Library: a standard large title with a + menu (Add a game, Installer, Steam library) and Settings in the top bar. Games are artwork-first tiles, most recently played first, each with its name, last-played time and a Play button.
Settings now uses the standard iOS grouped list.
Accent colours are now blue (default), indigo, teal, green, orange and pink.

summary: The stats overlay stops flickering.
fixed: The stats chip at the top of the game faded out and back in every second when it updated. Its text now changes in place, with no animation, and only when it actually differs.

summary: A new look.
added: Appearance in Settings: choose System, Dark or Light, and an accent colour (violet, blue, teal, green, coral, amber). It changes everywhere straight away.
Home screen: a big 'Continue playing' card for the game you played last, quick buttons for Add a game and Installer, and all other games in a grid below.
changed: New design throughout: soft near-black (or light) surfaces with a glow of the accent colour, rounded type, large rounded cards, gradient buttons and frosted-glass chips. The in-game controls are unchanged.

summary: Full first-run walkthrough and a choice of JIT method.
added: Setup walkthrough (7 pages): welcome; how JIT will be switched on; allow the connection; whether you can sign apps (for updating inside the app); Steam; first game; summary. Reopen any time from Settings > Setup guide.

JIT method choice: in the app with a pairing file, StikDebug, or another tool (the app waits and shows 'Waiting for JIT' until you switch it on). The app's own tunnel serves all three, so LocalDevVPN is no longer needed for StikDebug. Settings > Connection has a JIT method picker.

Signing certificate step: Yes (add .p12 + password + profile, and the update server address/token) or No (explains that new .ipa files have to be installed by hand), with a 'What's this?' page listing the pros and cons.
changed: First launch always shows the walkthrough (people who already had a pairing file and games are not interrupted). 'Finish setting up' stays on the home screen until you press Finish.

summary: Easier for newcomers: a setup guide and a simpler app.
added: Setup guide: on first launch (and any time from Settings) a four-step 'Let's get you ready' guide — pairing file (with step-by-step instructions for getting one), allow the connection, optional Steam sign-in, add your first game. Each step ticks itself off.
The library shows a 'Finish setting up' banner until the pairing file is in.
changed: Settings now shows only Performance (power mode), Controls, Sound, Pairing file, Updates and Log. Everything technical (swap and video memory, shader math, hot-phone override, Steam desktop switch, JIT and tunnel status, debugging) is behind 'Show advanced options' at the bottom.
The library's JIT, tunnel and power chips are hidden unless advanced options are on.
'Add a game' now says to import a game folder from Files.

summary: Factorio starts again.
fixed: Factorio (and other games using Windows picture drawing) stopped on start because gdiplus.dll had been left out of the app since 0.15.8. It is back, and the build now always includes it.

summary: Import a game folder from Files.
added: Add a game > Import a game folder from Files: pick the game's folder anywhere in Files (On My iPhone, iCloud Drive, a USB drive). The app copies it into its Windows drive (C:\Games\<name>) with a progress bar and the option to cancel, then adds the game, or asks which program starts it if there are several.

summary: Safer tunnel shut-off.
changed: The tunnel now turns off a few seconds after the game process has started (JIT is long finished by then) instead of the moment the helper reports done, so it can never be cut while JIT is still being set up.

summary: Tunnel turns on again.
fixed: The JIT tunnel could refuse to start with 'NEVPNErrorDomain error 2' (iOS had disabled its VPN setting). The setting is now re-read every time and turned back on if needed.

summary: The JIT tunnel only runs while a game starts.
changed: Play turns the tunnel on, and it turns off again as soon as JIT is ready (the debugger has detached), or if JIT fails before attaching. A tunnel left on by a closed or crashed run is turned off when the app opens.

summary: Steam test launch, Dock unaffected.
fixed: Restored the Dock's own installer shell (0.15.11 changed it by mistake).

summary: Steam client test launch fix.
fixed: The Steam client test launch used the 64-bit command shell and stopped at once (bad image format); it now uses the 32-bit shell so Steam gets the 32-bit session it needs.

summary: Steam client test launch.
added: The real Steam client (steam.exe on the Wine desktop) now starts through Wine's service manager with the options Madeira's own Steam test uses (no sandbox, software rendering, no crash monitor). Wine debug channel +sock records the first bytes of network connections.

summary: Launch options for each program.
added: Launch options: a field on every program's page for command-line options (for the real Steam client, -tcp makes it connect over plain TCP instead of web sockets).

summary: More Windows system libraries for launchers.
added: Added Windows system libraries that launchers and installers ask for (Restart Manager, cabinet, crypto, text, network helpers). The Epic Games Launcher stopped at its first start because RstrtMgr.dll was missing.

summary: Epic Games Launcher gets past its first instruction.
fixed: Programs that ship their own Microsoft ucrtbase.dll (the Epic Games Launcher does) crashed before starting on the Wine desktop. The app now sets those copies aside (renamed to ucrtbase.dll.f4off) so the built-in one is used.

summary: More installer click diagnosis.
fixed: Setup windows that answer a click with 'activate and swallow the click' no longer lose the press on the Wine desktop; the log also records what the window answered.

summary: Installer buttons now react to taps.
fixed: Setup windows (NSIS, Epic Games Launcher .msi) ignored every tap on their buttons: the press was swallowed when Windows could not make the window the active one. The press is now delivered anyway.

summary: Message trace for installers that do not react to taps.
added: With Settings > Debugging > Wine debug channels set to +msg, the log now also lists every message each Windows window receives, to find why some installers (NSIS, Epic) ignore taps.

summary: Installers draw their windows and 32-bit installers start.
fixed: Installers (Epic Games Launcher .msi, NSIS) that open their window hidden showed nothing or only part of it; every window is now fully repainted when it is shown.
32-bit installers (for example the GOG Fallout 2 one) crashed on their first window; fixed in the 32-bit Windows call layer.

summary: Wine debug channels for diagnosis.
added: Settings > Debugging > Wine debug channels: for example +msg records window messages in the log. Leave it empty normally.

summary: Debug switch for Windows window pictures.
added: Settings > Debugging > Save window pictures: saves what each Windows window really contains to Files > Porthole > surfdump, to diagnose installers and tools that look wrong.

summary: Run Windows installers.
added: Run an installer (home screen): pick a setup .exe or .msi from Files. The app copies it into the Windows folder tree, runs it on Wine's desktop so its windows are drawn, and (after the app is reopened) offers to add what it installed to your library. .msi files run through the 32-bit installer service.
Show Windows windows (Wine desktop) switch on each game's page, for launchers and tools that draw ordinary windows.

summary: Look sensitivity for first-person mode.
added: Look sensitivity: a slider in Settings (the default for every game) and on each game's page (that game only). The default is 2.4x; the range is 0.4x to 8x.
In first-person mode the in-game Menu has Slower / Faster buttons that change the look speed immediately and remember it for that game.

summary: Fixes the crash when pressing Play.
fixed: Pressing Play crashed the app in 0.14.0: the new first-person controls changed how the movement stick is created, and the game screen's normal stick hit a deliberate trap.

summary: First-person touch controls.
added: First person controls layout (game page > Controls): left stick walks, drag anywhere on the right to look, FIRE and ALT buttons (the two mouse buttons), Jump, Use (E), Duck, Run, Reload, Tab, Esc.
A Look / Menu button (top right) switches the screen between looking around and acting as a normal mouse, so you can tap through menus.

summary: Game pages, per-game settings, lighter logging.
added: Every game card shows how it starts (STEAM or DIRECT) and whether it is 32- or 64-bit, plus when you last played and for how long.

A game page (tap the ... on a card): program, launch mode, Steam app, size on disk, last played, time played. From it you can verify and update a Steam game's files, delete its files, or remove it from the library.

Per-game settings: power mode, keep-mode-when-hot, swap tier and coverage, video memory, audio buffer, precise shader math and the Wine desktop display can each be set for one game. "Global" follows Settings.
A controls layout choice per game (First person arrives in the next update).
changed: The graphics layer's memory report now prints once every 10 seconds instead of every few frames: hundreds of thousands fewer log lines per session, so less CPU and heat.
Changing the power mode during a game only changes that session; the saved choice stays.

summary: Back to the Wine desktop for Steam games.
changed: Steam games run on the Wine desktop again by default. The single-display mode from 0.12.7 crashed the 32-bit game while it was starting, so it is now an experiment you can turn on in Settings > Steam games.

summary: One display for Steam games.
added: Steam games now draw straight into the app's game view, like direct games, instead of a separate Wine desktop display. Controls, touch and rotation work the same everywhere. Settings > Steam games has a switch to go back to the Wine desktop display if a game needs it.

summary: Black screen after rotating (Steam games) fixed.
fixed: Steam games started through Dock went black when the phone was rotated, with the game still running underneath. In those sessions Wine draws the game in its own desktop layer, and the app kept pulling its own black game view on top of it each time the screen laid out. The app now leaves that layer alone and keeps only the controls on top.

summary: Status text fits the screen.
fixed: The long "Steam started the game. Loading..." message was cut off at the edge of the screen; it now wraps.

summary: Rotation fix for Steam (desktop) games.
added: The log now records the display layout (`[display] apply ...`) each time it changes.
fixed: Steam games started through Dock showed a black screen (with the controls) after the phone was rotated, even though the game kept running. The game view now follows the game's real display size, tells the desktop compositor where the picture goes, and re-applies the layout again just after a rotation settles, the way Madeira's own game view does.

summary: Swap tier and video memory settings.
added: Settings > Memory: Swap tier (1-4 GB) keeps big chunks of game data in a file on the phone's storage, where iOS does not count them, so memory-hungry games are less likely to be closed. Choose what it covers (large allocations, all 1 MB+, or 1 MB+ and overflow).
Settings > Memory: Video memory, how much graphics memory games are told they have (Automatic, 1.5-4 GB).

summary: Keep your power mode when the phone is hot.
added: Settings > Performance > "Keep my mode when the phone is hot": stops the automatic switch to Battery saver (30 FPS + Eco) at "hot". Eco puts the game on the slow cores, so this helps long loads. At "very hot" Battery saver is still forced to protect the phone.

summary: Clearer Steam launch status.
fixed: The on-screen message no longer stays on "Steam is checking your licence" after Steam has confirmed it. It now says the licence is confirmed, then that the game is loading.

summary: 32-bit games, and Steam games that check your licence.
added: 32-bit Windows programs: the 32-bit Windows system files are now in the app (built from the same Wine source), so 32-bit games and installers can run. A tiny test program is included: add C:\windows\syswow64\hello-x86.exe in Add a game and check the log for "hello from a 32-bit PE".

Steam launching through Madeira Dock: games you download from the Steam screen start through Valve's own Steam client files, which check your licence. Download the client files (about 73 MB) from the Steam screen once; nothing is bypassed.
Per-game switch (press and hold a card): Run directly (skip Steam) or Start through Steam.
Steam shows what is happening while a game starts (starting Steam, checking your licence) and explains failures.
changed: The runtime is on Madeira's newest source (Oct 1).

summary: Steam downloads keep going in the background.
added: Leave the app while a game downloads: on iOS 26+ it keeps running with iOS's own progress card (with a stop control). If iOS refuses, you get a short grace period, then a clean pause that continues when you reopen the app.
Notifications when a download finishes, fails or pauses while you are away (the app asks permission when the first download starts).
Downloads wait while a game is running so they do not slow it down, then continue by themselves.

summary: Steam sign-in survives leaving the app.
fixed: Approving a Steam sign-in in the Steam app and coming back no longer fails with "No internet connection". iOS cuts the app's connection while you are away; the sign-in now just keeps waiting and finishes when you return.

summary: Download your Steam games.
added: Steam library: sign in with your Steam account (name and password with Steam Guard, or a QR code) and see every Windows game you own.
Install, pause, resume and remove games from the Steam screen. Finished games appear in your library with a Play button and their Steam picture.
Updates for installed games when Steam has a newer build; interrupted downloads resume where they stopped.
A Steam panel on the home screen shows the download that is running.

summary: Game cards show their Steam artwork.
added: Each game card now shows its picture from Steam. The app finds the game by name (or by its folder / exe name) once, remembers it, and caches the image on the phone.
Press and hold a card > Choose Steam artwork... to search by hand if the automatic match is wrong, or pick No artwork.
changed: Cards are a little taller to show the picture.

summary: New library home screen.
added: A dark, industrial library: a card for each game with a big PLAY button, a status strip (JIT, tunnel, power mode) and an Add a game card.
Settings screen (gear, top right) holds performance, sound, JIT / tunnel and the Updates and Log pages.
An update banner appears on the home screen when a new build is on your Hub.
Launch problems show as a banner you can dismiss.
changed: The cluttered list of switches on the library is gone; everything moved into Settings.
Tap the power-mode chip to cycle Performance / Balanced / Battery saver.

summary: Shorter audio breaks.
changed: After an audio stall the sound now rebuilds its cushion by playing very slightly slower for a few seconds, instead of inserting silence.
fixed: Audio breaks got longer the bigger the Audio buffer was: the driver refilled the cushion with silence after every stall. A break is now only the part of the stall the cushion could not cover.

summary: Fixes choppy audio.
added: Audio buffer setting (library screen): extra buffered sound, default 80 ms. Raise it if you still hear glitches, lower it if effects feel late.
The log prints an audio underrun count every 10 seconds.
fixed: Choppy, crackling audio: the game only keeps ~10 ms of sound queued, so any short stall in the emulated audio thread produced a glitch. The audio driver now keeps a cushion and refills it after a stall.

summary: Controls rework: much more of the screen is yours.
added: Menu button (top left) opens Keyboard, Power, Hide controls, ? and Close game.
••• button opens the extra keys (Q R T M G, Space, Shift/Ctrl/Alt, Enter, Del, Zoom, Right mode) only when you want them.
changed: Only E (inventory), F, Tab and Esc stay on screen, as small round buttons in the bottom right.
The movement stick is about 30% smaller.
The number keys 1-0 are gone; tap the quickbar on screen instead.

summary: Fixes the black world at dusk and dawn.
changed: Precise shader math is now off by default (it made no difference); the switch is still on the library screen.
fixed: The world no longer goes black while day turns to night and back: the graphics layer was silently ignoring the copy that builds the game's day/night colour table (a 2D image into slices of a 3D texture).

summary: Diagnostics for the dusk/dawn black world.
added: Extra logging of 3D-texture activity in the graphics layer (the day/night colour tables), so the next log shows what goes wrong at dusk and dawn.

summary: Test fix for the black world at dusk and dawn.
added: Precise shader math (library screen, on by default): the shader translator uses exact math instead of fast approximations, to test whether that stops the world going black between day and night. Applies the next time a game starts. Shaders are recompiled once, so the first launch after updating loads slower.

summary: Real touch gestures for the game.
added: Gestures on the game: tap = left click; drag = left button held (belts, selection boxes); press and hold = right button held (mine / remove), and you can drag while holding; two-finger tap = right click; pinch = zoom.
A ? button in the top bar lists the gestures.
Right mode: tap and drag use the right button and a two-finger tap uses the left.
changed: Touching no longer clicks straight away: the cursor moves to your finger at once (so hover works) and the click happens when you lift, so a drag, a hold or a two-finger gesture never leaves a stray click.
The movement stick moved up and in from the bottom-left corner, where Factorio draws its quickbar.
Mouse: Left/Right is now "Right mode".

summary: The telemetry readout can always be brought back.
changed: The readout remembers whether it was compact, full or hidden.
fixed: Tapping the readout to hide it removed the only thing you could tap to bring it back. Hidden now leaves a small "Stats" chip.

summary: Top-bar buttons receive taps again; less flicker.
added: The full readout also shows how often the HUD was updated and re-attached, to help track the flicker if it remains.
changed: The HUD only reacts to real state changes and only re-orders its views when the order is wrong.
fixed: Esc, Tab, Keyboard, Controls, Power and the readout did not respond: the full-screen container for the stick and key panel sat on top of the top bar and swallowed every tap meant for it. Reproduced and verified in the iOS Simulator.

summary: Key presses last long enough to be seen, and an input counter to diagnose them.
added: The full telemetry view (tap the readout twice) has an Input line: keys sent, the last key, and touches on the game.
changed: A key press now lasts 70 ms instead of zero. Typed text goes out one character every 70 ms.
fixed: Buttons such as Tab could be missed by games that read the keyboard once per frame, because down and up were sent in the same instant.

summary: Telemetry overlay and on-screen controls.
added: Telemetry in the game (tap it to cycle compact / full / hidden): FPS with the worst recent value and frame time, CPU load and thread count, app memory and how much is left before iOS would close the app, GPU memory, heat, battery with a drain rate, Low Power Mode and the power mode. Also logged every 15 s and saved every 5 s to telemetry.csv in the app's Files folder.
Movement stick (W/A/S/D, eight directions) and a key panel: E Q R F T M G, Space (hold), Shift / Ctrl / Alt (tap to latch), Enter, Del and the number row 1-0.
Esc, Tab and a Keyboard button (the iOS keyboard, for typing such as a world name) in the top bar; Controls hides or shows the stick and key panel.
Mouse: Left / Right switch (Right holds the right button while your finger is down) and Zoom + / Zoom - (mouse wheel).
changed: The Power button moved into the top bar.

summary: Power modes: less heat and battery use.
added: Three power modes (tap Power in the game): Performance (60 FPS), Balanced (30 FPS, the default) and Battery saver (30 FPS plus Eco, which moves the game's threads to the efficiency cores at lower clocks).
A thermal guard: when iOS reports the phone as hot, the game drops to Battery saver by itself until it cools.
A one-line readout in the game: FPS, thermal state and the mode in force. It is also written to the log every 15 seconds.
changed: Factorio now draws at 30 FPS by default. Its simulation still runs at 60 updates per second.

summary: Fixes the JIT pool allocation failure that forced a relaunch.
fixed: "JIT pool allocation failed. Force-quit and relaunch": when the biggest free gap in memory was below the game window, the pool was sized for that gap and then the code blocked that same gap, leaving only the forbidden guest window (BAD POOL ... guest 64G window, three times). The gap is now left open when the pool only fits there.
The log notes when this case applies ("f4-0003").

summary: The update download bar moves.
changed: The Updates screen shows a percentage and the size while downloading and while sending the signed copy to your Hub.
fixed: The download progress bar stayed empty and the step appeared to skip. iOS never delivers download progress to the callback the old transport used; the app now uses a session-level one. (Measured: 0 progress updates before, 114 after, same file.)

summary: JIT without LocalDevVPN: the app has its own tunnel.
added: A built-in loopback tunnel (a Network Extension) that gives the JIT helper the route to the device's debug service. It starts automatically when you enable JIT, and the library screen shows its state with a manual switch.
If the tunnel cannot start, JIT is still attempted, so LocalDevVPN keeps working as before.
changed: The tunnel replaces any other VPN while it is on (iOS allows one at a time), including Tailscale.

summary: The Updates screen shows when it last checked.
added: "Up to date" now says when the last check happened, so it is clear whether the app really asked your Hub.

summary: Turn on JIT from inside the app.
added: In-app JIT: a helper extension attaches a debugger to the app for you, so StikDebug is no longer needed. Import your pairing file once (library screen), turn on LocalDevVPN, then Play.
The JIT row on the library screen shows whether a pairing file is imported.
changed: Play uses in-app JIT when a pairing file is imported, and falls back to StikDebug when it is not.

summary: Update the app from inside the app.
added: Updates screen: checks your Hub for a newer build, downloads it, signs it on the device with your own certificate and provisioning profile, and hands it to iOS to install.
Certificate (.p12) and profile (.mobileprovision) import, with expiry warnings. The signing code is the Launcher's own.

summary: Touch input reaches the game.
fixed: Taps and drags moved the cursor by tiny relative amounts; pointer events now carry the absolute flag the runtime requires.
